prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read temperature from an LM35 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 10-bit ADC, wired via SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8-11), using the pigpio library (not wiringPi or any deprecated library) for SPI communication. The LM35 output is 10 mV/°C; the MCP3008 VREF is 3.3 V. Use the MCP3008 SPI protocol: start bit (0x01), then single-ended mode bit plus channel number (channel 0 -> 0x80), then a don't-care byte, extracting the result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]. Read the temperature every 5 seconds, log each reading to the console in the format 'Temperature: XX.XX °C', and maintain a circular buffer of 120 float entries in memory; every 5 seconds overwrite the entire circular buffer to a binary file 'temp_log.dat' (opened with mode 'wb+') so the file always contains exactly 120 float values, with the oldest data overwritten when the buffer wraps. Check pigpio initialization, SPI open, and each SPI transfer; on SPI transfer failure, print an error and skip that reading rather than exiting; on file open failure, print an error and continue without logging to file. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that logs ambient light and sound levels with timestamps to a file named "environmental_log.txt". Read ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, and read sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI using /dev/spidev0.0. Use the standard Linux i2c-dev API for I2C and the standard Linux spidev API for SPI; do not use the wiringPi library. Sample both sensors every 1 second and format each log entry as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]". Handle I2C and SPI errors gracefully, including sensor-absent or bus-error conditions, without crashing. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, terminate gracefully and cleanly release all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor module connected to GPIO 17, using the libgpiod library. Initialize the GPIO line for input with pull-down enabled, then continuously poll the sensor every 1 second. The sensor's digital output is active HIGH when flame is detected (threshold adjustable via an onboard potentiometer) and operates at 3.3 V logic level. Log each timestamped HIGH/LOW reading to "flame_events.log" in CSV format: timestamp, pin, state. When flame is detected, print an alarm message to stdout. Use only the libgpiod API (gpiod_line_*, gpiod_chip_*) — not sysfs, wiringPi, or pigpio. Check every libgpiod call, print error messages to stderr, and exit with a non-zero status on failure. Clean up GPIO resources on normal exit and on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature from a TMP36 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, mode 0, 500 kHz), converts the reading to Celsius, and outputs a proportional voltage via an MCP4725 I2C DAC at address 0x62 on bus 1. Linearly map the temperature range 0C to 50C to a DAC output of 0V to 3.3V. Use the pigpio library for all GPIO, SPI and I2C access. Check every initialization, SPI transfer, I2C write and file operation; handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully with retries and clear error messages. Log each reading — timestamp, raw ADC value, temperature in C, and DAC voltage — to "temperature_log.txt" and also print it to stdout, sampling every 0.5 seconds. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully: close SPI and I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio. Do not use wiringPi or other deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads moisture levels from three DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 analog resistive sensors via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0, SPI mode 0, 1 MHz clock), using the pigpio library. Read all three sensors on MCP3008 single-ended channels 0, 1 and 2, and convert each ADC value (0-1023) to a moisture percentage using moisture = (1.0 - (adc_value / 1023.0)) * 100.0, where 0% is dry and 100% is wet. Log timestamped readings ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "soil_data.txt" in append mode, one line per sensor per cycle, with a 60-second sleep interval between cycles. If spiOpen or spiXfer fails, print an error message and exit with code 1; if a sensor read produces an invalid ADC value, print an error and continue. On SIGINT, close SPI, close the log file, terminate pigpio, and print a goodbye message, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths. Use only pigpio functions (spiOpen, spiXfer, spiClose, gpioInitialise, gpioTerminate, gpioDelay) — do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to sequentially activate and deactivate four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relays connected to BCM GPIO pins 17, 22, 23 and 24, simulating a basic light sequencer. Use libgpiod calls (gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) with error checking on every call. Initially set all relay pins inactive (LOW, assuming active-high relay modules). In a loop, activate each relay in sequence for 1 second, then deactivate it, with a 1-second delay between relays, repeating the full cycle indefinitely until interrupted. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines before exiting. Include no SPI, ADC, temperature-sensor, or logging functionality — the task is relay sequencing only. Use only standard C libraries and libgpiod, not wiringPi or pigpio, and include clear comments explaining each step.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor's analog output through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0 on GPIO8, mode 0, 1 MHz clock), reading MCP3008 channel 0. When the sound level exceeds a threshold of 500 (10-bit ADC value), turn on an LED connected to GPIO16, log the timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "sound_events.log", and keep the LED on for 500 ms. Read the ADC every 10 ms in the main loop, applying a debounce delay after each trigger. Handle SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selection, and GPIO initialization errors gracefully, checking every pigpio call and file operation. Install a signal handler for SIGINT to cleanly release resources on exit: close SPI, terminate pigpio, and turn off the LED. Use the pigpio library, not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library for GPIO and SPI that reads a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor (analog output) through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (channel 0, 1 MHz, mode 0), and drives an L298N-based DC motor to automatically close a window when rain is detected. Wire the motor driver as IN1=GPIO17, IN2=GPIO18, ENA=GPIO27 with PWM (range 255, duty 150). Read the rain sensor with the standard 3-byte MCP3008 single-ended transfer: tx[0]=0x01, tx[1]=(0x08|channel)<<4, tx[2]=0x00, parsing the 10-bit result from the low 2 bits of rx[1] and all of rx[2]. Convert the ADC value (0-1023) to a rain level (0-10) so that ADC 1023 maps to rain level 0 (dry) and ADC 0 maps to rain level 10 (heaviest rain), since the sensor outputs higher voltage when dry. Poll every 1 second, and log each timestamped rain reading to "rain_log.txt" in append mode, flushing after every write. When the rain level is at or above a threshold of 5, close the window by driving the motor forward (IN1=1, IN2=0, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds; when it drops below the threshold, open the window by driving the motor in reverse (IN1=0, IN2=1, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds. The window starts in the open state. Handle pigpio initialization failures, SPI open failures, and log file open failures with clear error messages and proper cleanup, checking every init, syscall and I/O return value, and handling SPI transfer and log write failures without crashing. Install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag for graceful shutdown: stop the motor, close SPI, close the log file, and terminate pigpio, releasing all resources on every exit path. Use only the pigpio library, not wiringPi; the program should compile with gcc -o rain rain.c -lpigpio -lrt -lpthread.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library that implements a basic clap detector with a MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier (with AGC) whose output is read as an analog level on GPIO26 via pigpio's bit-banged ADC sampling. When the signal exceeds a threshold of approximately 0.7 x 3.3 V = 2.31 V, corresponding to a raw 10-bit ADC reading of about 700 out of 1023, turn on an LED on GPIO16 for 500 ms, print a timestamped detection message to the console, and apply a 50 ms debounce to avoid false triggers. Check the return values of pigpio initialization, ADC setup, and GPIO mode configuration, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully. Install a SIGINT handler for clean shutdown that turns off the LED and terminates pigpio. Run continuously until interrupted with Ctrl+C, using C11 and avoiding deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads distance from a Sharp GP2Y0A21YK0F IR distance sensor using the sysfs GPIO interface on GPIO 17. Because the sensor's real output is analog and this exercise has no ADC available, treat GPIO 17 as a digital input reading 0 or 1, convert that to a placeholder voltage (0V for low, 3.3V for high), and then convert the voltage to distance using distance (mm) = A / voltage + B, with A = 26.0 and B = -6.0. Log each reading with a timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "distance_log.txt" in append mode. Implement a proximity-based pet feeder activation: if the computed distance is below 200 mm, print "Feeder Activated" to the console; otherwise print "Feeder Idle". Handle GPIO file open or read errors gracefully by printing an error and retrying after 1 second. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, unexport GPIO 17 and exit cleanly. The program should run continuously until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library, together with the standard Linux spidev SPI interface, to read analog soil moisture data from a Vegetronix VH400 sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, SCLK=GPIO11, MOSI=GPIO10, MISO=GPIO9), configured for single-ended mode on channel 0. Using calibrated ADC values of dry=800 and wet=300, if the moisture level drops below 30%, activate a 12V submersible water pump connected to GPIO17 through an active-high relay. Log each reading to "soil_moisture.log" with a timestamp, the moisture percentage, and the pump status (ON/OFF), sampling every 60 seconds continuously. Check every initialization step (libgpiod, SPI, log file), handle sensor read failures gracefully, and validate ADC values. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully by turning off the pump, closing the log file, and releasing all GPIO resources. Use only libgpiod and the standard Linux spidev SPI interface — do not use bcm2835 or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads analog voltage from a DRV5055-A1 Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI, using the Linux spidev interface on /dev/spidev0.0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, 8 bits per word, together with libgpiod (gpiochip0, line 8) to manually drive chip-select low during each SPI transfer and high afterward. Hardware wiring: MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 3.3 V rail; MCP3008 DOUT to GPIO 10, DIN to GPIO 9, CLK to GPIO 11, and CS/SHDN to GPIO 8; DRV5055-A1 VOUT to MCP3008 channel 0, DRV5055 VCC to 3.3 V. The MCP3008 is a 10-bit ADC (0-1023) with VREF = 3.3 V, so compute Vout_mV = adc_value * 3300 / 1023. The DRV5055-A1 has a sensitivity of 100 mV/mT and a quiescent output of VCC/2 = 1650 mV, so compute the magnetic field B (mT) = (Vout_mV - 1650) / 100. Sample every 500 ms and append a CSV row to "magnetic_log.txt" as <unix_epoch>,<B_mt_two_decimals>. Use integer arithmetic internally for the field calculation and print the floating-point result with two decimal places in the log. Include all necessary headers such as stdint.h. Check every open, ioctl, SPI transfer, fopen, and fprintf call and propagate errors; if an ADC read fails, log the error to stderr, skip that sample, and continue the loop. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly, releasing the GPIO line, closing the gpiochip, closing the SPI file descriptor, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library that reads analog voltage from a TI DRV5055VA Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8, 9, 10, 11), with the sensor output wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended) and the sensor powered at 3.3 V. Initialize pigpio and SPI, handling initialization failures. Read the 10-bit MCP3008 value (0-1023) and convert it to voltage: V = ADC * 3.3 / 1023. Scale the voltage to magnetic field strength in mT using the DRV5055VA's ratiometric characteristics: quiescent output = VCC/2, and sensitivity at 3.3 V = 2.5 * 3.3/5 = 1.65 mV/mT, so field_mT = (voltage - VCC/2) * 1000 / sensitivity_mV_per_mT. Log each timestamped field-strength reading to "magnetic_log.txt" in append mode. If the field exceeds a threshold of 10.0 mT, turn on an LED on GPIO21; otherwise turn it off. Loop with a 100 ms delay between readings, using real ADC reads rather than simulated values. Handle SIGINT for graceful cleanup: close SPI, turn off the LED, and terminate pigpio. Check every SPI open, ADC read, and file open for errors. Use only pigpio for GPIO and SPI — do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor soil moisture with a DFRobot resistive soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0 (CE0, mode 0, 1 MHz), with the sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 single-ended input channel 0. Initialize pigpio and open SPI with proper error handling. Every 60 seconds, read the ADC value using the MCP3008's single-ended protocol: start bit 0x01, single-ended mode bit 0x80, with the channel-selection bits in byte 1, and parse the 10-bit result from bits 1-2 of rx_buf[1] and all of rx_buf[2]. Log each reading with a timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") and the raw ADC value to "moisture_log.txt" in append mode; on an ADC read failure (return -1), log an error line with a timestamp to the same file instead. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to gracefully close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit. Include robust error checking for every initialization, syscall, and I/O operation, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod for GPIO control (chip 0, line 17) and the Linux spidev SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) for ADC communication, to read analog current values from a Melexis MLX91209 (the analog-output version) connected to BCM GPIO pin 17. The MLX91209 outputs an analog voltage proportional to current (0-5V range, sensitivity approximately 100 mV/A). Since the Raspberry Pi has no analog input, digitize the sensor output using an external MCP3008 ADC on channel 0 over SPI. Log the current readings, in amperes, and timestamps to "current_log.txt" in CSV format (timestamp,current_A), reading and logging at 1-second intervals. Check every initialization step — SPI, GPIO, and file operations — and handle sensor-absent or communication failures gracefully. Use signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean termination, releasing the GPIO line, closing the SPI handle, and closing the log file on exit. Do not use the sysfs GPIO interface or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read current from a Melexis MLX91211 analog-output current sensor via an MCP3008 SPI ADC. Wire the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus: CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11, with MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 5V rail and AGND/DGND tied to Pi GND. Wire the MLX91211 analog output to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended), with MLX91211 VDD from the Pi's 5V pin and GND to Pi GND. The MLX91211 output is ratiometric: 2.5V (VDD/2) at zero current and 5.0V (VDD) at full-scale +50A; linearly interpolate between those points. Initialize pigpio with gpioInitialise(), printing an error and exiting non-zero on failure. Open SPI0 (ce=0) at 1 MHz, mode 0 with spiOpen, terminating pigpio and exiting non-zero on failure. In a loop, read MCP3008 channel 0 with a 3-byte SPI transfer tx = {0x01, 0x80 | (channel<<4), 0x00} via spiXfer, computing the 10-bit result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]; on an SPI transfer error, print a diagnostic and skip that sample. Convert the raw code (0-1023) to voltage (0-5V), then to current using current = (voltage - 2.5) * (50.0 / 2.5); if voltage falls outside [0, 5V], print a warning and skip the sample. Every 100 ms (gpioDelay(100000)), append a timestamped line to "current_log.txt" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS XX.XX A", flushing after each write; on file-open failure, close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit non-zero. Install a SIGINT handler that sets a volatile flag so the loop exits cleanly; on exit, close the log file, call spiClose, and call gpioTerminate. Use only pigpio's spiOpen, spiXfer, and spiClose functions, include the necessary headers such as unistd.h, and comment the code clearly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with two Omron B5W-DB01 diffuse reflective sensors using the libgpiod library. Each sensor has a single digital output only — active-low, open-collector with an internal pull-up, where object present = LOW and no object = HIGH; the sensor has no analog light-intensity output. Connect sensor 1's output to GPIO4 and sensor 2's output to GPIO17. Check every libgpiod call (gpiod_chip_open_by_number, gpiod_line_request_input, etc.) and exit with a clear error message on failure. Debounce each read by sampling 5 times with 2 ms between reads and accepting the majority value. Log each sensor's state (0 = object present, 1 = no object) to the console once per second. If both sensors report object present simultaneously, print the warning "ALERT: Both sensors detect object". Handle SIGINT to release all GPIO resources (gpiod_line_release, gpiod_chip_close) and exit cleanly. Do not use pigpio, wiringPi, or any deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to periodically read analog moisture levels from a YL-69 soil moisture sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0, CE0, at a 1 MHz baud rate, with the sensor on MCP3008 single-ended channel 0. Use the SPI command format: start bit 0x01, then a single-ended-plus-channel-select byte 0x80 | (channel << 4), then a dummy byte 0x00, reading the 10-bit ADC value as ((rx_buf[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx_buf[2]. Calibrate so that ADC value 300 represents very dry soil and 800 represents very wet soil, converting to a moisture percentage with 100.0 - ((adc - 300) / (800 - 300)) * 100.0, clamped to [0, 100]. Every 60 seconds, append a reading to "soil_moisture_log.csv" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,moisture_percentage" (e.g. "2025-03-15 14:30:00,45.23") and also print it to the console. Check every pigpio initialization, SPI open, SPI transfer, and file open call; on an SPI transfer failure, print an error and retry after a delay without exiting; on a file-open failure, print an error and continue. Use a volatile sig_atomic_t flag set by a SIGINT handler to close the SPI handle, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly, releasing resources on every path — for example, if SPI open fails, terminate pigpio before returning. Include the headers pigpio.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, unistd.h, time.h, signal.h, and string.h. Define constants SPI_CHANNEL (0), SPI_BAUD (1000000), MCP3008_CHANNEL (0), READ_DELAY (60), MIN_ADC (300), MAX_ADC (800), and LOG_FILE ("soil_moisture_log.csv"). Implement functions read_mcp3008(int channel), calculate_moisture_level(int adc_value), log_data(double moisture_level), signal_handler(int signal), and spi_setup(spi_config_t config); in main, initialize pigpio, open SPI, register the signal handler, loop until the termination flag is set reading the ADC, calculating moisture, logging data, and delaying 60 seconds each cycle, then close SPI and terminate pigpio on cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, using the pigpio library, that detects motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor connected to BCM GPIO17 and triggers a camera snapshot via the libcamera-still command-line utility. Initialize pigpio and verify success; configure GPIO17 as input with a pull-down resistor, and poll it every 50 ms. After a state change, apply a 200 ms debounce delay and re-read the GPIO to confirm the state. On motion detection, capture a 1280x720 JPEG image with an ISO 8601 timestamp filename, saved to /home/pi/security_cam/; construct the output path safely with snprintf and verify the target directory exists before capture. Execute libcamera-still via fork and execvp (never system()), checking the child's exit status and treating a non-zero exit as a capture error. Log all key events — startup, motion detected, capture success or failure, and shutdown — to syslog. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the main loop, release pigpio resources, and close syslog. Do not use wiringPi or placeholder camera functions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that captures grayscale images from an Arducam OV5647 CSI camera module using the V4L2 API — the kernel interface exposed through libcamera's V4L2 compatibility layer, not libcamera's C++ API directly. Save each frame as a raw grayscale .pgm file, named sequentially (image_0001.pgm, image_0002.pgm, etc.). Open the V4L2 device given on the command line, defaulting to /dev/video0. Set the format to 640x480 using V4L2_PIX_FMT_GREY (8-bit grayscale), and use memory-mapped (V4L2_MEMORY_MMAP) streaming with a single buffer. Handle every open(), ioctl(), mmap(), fwrite(), and close() call, printing strerror(errno) on failure, and handle EAGAIN gracefully when dequeuing buffers using select() with a 2-second timeout to avoid infinite loops. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to stop streaming and unmap buffers safely. The program should capture frames continuously until a signal is received or a fatal error occurs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that captures an MJPEG video stream from a USB webcam connected at /dev/video0. Configure the video capture for a resolution of 640x480, using the V4L2 API directly rather than the libv4l2 wrapper library. For every captured frame, log its timestamp in microseconds to a file named "frame_log.txt", writing each entry in the format "seconds.microseconds". Use memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers for frame capture, and handle input and output asynchronously with select() so the program never blocks indefinitely waiting for a frame. Implement robust error handling for every V4L2 ioctl call, every file operation, and every memory mapping, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including a graceful shutdown triggered by SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (Broadcom BCM2711, e.g. Pi 4) that captures video from the CSI camera, exposed as /dev/video0 via V4L2, and streams it over UDP to a target IP address and port given as command-line arguments (./program <server_ip> <server_port>). Use V4L2 MMAP streaming with 4 buffers at 640x480 YUYV format. Fragment each frame into UDP datagrams of at most 65000 bytes, each prefixed with a small header containing the frame index, fragment index, total fragment count, and payload size, so the receiver can reassemble frames. Handle errors at every syscall — open, ioctl, mmap, socket, and sendto — and exit gracefully on failure. Run until SIGINT or SIGTERM is received, then cleanly stop streaming, munmap all buffers, and close all descriptors.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi to capture a single 1920x1080 JPEG image from a USB camera at /dev/video0 and save it to "image.jpg", using the V4L2 API with memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers. Open the device in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK) so VIDIOC_DQBUF blocks until a frame is ready. Query device capabilities and verify V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are supported. Request the format V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG at 1920x1080 with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, request 4 MMAP buffers, and query, mmap, and queue each one. Start streaming, dequeue one frame, verify buf.bytesused > 0, and write the raw MJPEG bytes directly to disk with no re-encoding. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths: stop streaming, munmap all mapped buffers, free the buffer array, close the file, and close the device fd. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly tears down streaming and releases resources. Check every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen return value, printing a descriptive error via perror/errno on failure. Do not use any external image libraries.

Write a C program using the libgpiod library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 and the tilt servo to GPIO5. Four push-buttons, wired active-low with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: GPIO6 moves tilt up, GPIO7 moves tilt down, GPIO8 moves pan left, and GPIO9 moves pan right. Generate software PWM through libgpiod with a 50 Hz period (20 ms) and pulse widths between 1 and 2 ms, expressed as duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000. Start both the pan and tilt servos at the mid-position value of 75. Each button press increments or decrements the corresponding servo's position by 5 units, clamped to the range [25, 125], polling all four buttons every 50 ms. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, handling chip-open and line-request failures, and cleanly release all GPIO resources when SIGINT is received.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi (Bookworm, 64-bit) that captures a single frame from a USB camera at /dev/video0, applies a 5x5 box-blur filter, and saves the result as a JPEG. Use the V4L2 MMAP API correctly: request buffers, mmap, queue, streamon, dequeue, streamoff, munmap, free buffers, and close the fd. Set the format to 640x480 YUYV, and use select() with a 2-second timeout for frame readiness. Convert the captured YUYV frame to RGB24, then apply a 5x5 box blur (kernel radius 2) with edge clamping. Save the blurred result as a JPEG at quality 75 using libjpeg, with an output filename of the form capture_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg. Handle SIGINT cleanly. Check every syscall and allocation; on error, print to stderr and clean up all resources. Do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi, running a 32-bit or 64-bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active, that queries a connected CSI camera at /dev/video0 and prints its supported resolutions, frame rates, and whether autofocus is supported. Use the V4L2 API: open the device, query capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerate frame sizes with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES, and enumerate frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS. Check every ioctl return value, and handle the cases where the device node does not exist or cannot be opened, where the camera does not support frame-size or interval enumeration, and where the focus control is not present. Print a clear summary to stdout and exit with a non-zero code on fatal errors.

Write a C program using the pigpio library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two standard hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: pan servo on GPIO4, tilt servo on GPIO5. Four push-buttons, active-low and wired to ground with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: UP on GPIO6, DOWN on GPIO7, LEFT on GPIO8, RIGHT on GPIO9. Servos expect a 50 Hz PWM signal with pulse widths between 1000 microseconds and 2000 microseconds; initialize both servos to the center position of 1500 microseconds. While a button is held, increment or decrement the corresponding servo position by 10 microseconds per loop iteration (50 ms loop delay), clamped to the 1000-2000 microsecond range. Use only pigpio — not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to detect motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). Initialize pigpio and configure GPIO17 as input with a pull-down resistor, checking and handling initialization failures; poll it every 100 ms, applying a 2-second debounce after each motion event. When motion is detected, capture a timestamped JPEG snapshot (640x480, quality 85) using the Raspberry Pi Camera Module v2 via the libcamera-still command-line tool, saving it to a directory named "motion_captures" (creating it if it does not exist, handling EEXIST gracefully). The program takes a server IP and port as command-line arguments and sends a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number to http://<server_ip>:<server_port>/upload using libcurl. Call curl_global_init exactly once at startup and curl_global_cleanup at exit. Check all system calls, libcurl operations, and file operations for errors, printing diagnostic messages to stderr. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, calling gpioTerminate() and curl_global_cleanup().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a PIR motion sensor (HC-SR501) connected to BCM GPIO17 (physical pin 11) to trigger the Raspberry Pi Camera Module v2 to capture and save a timestamped JPEG image to /home/pi/images. Use libgpiod (v2) for GPIO input and invoke the libcamera-still CLI utility for image capture. Open the GPIO chip and claim GPIO17 as input with edge-falling or edge-rising detection, applying a 50 ms debounce via a falling-edge wait with timeout. On motion detection, generate a timestamped filename in the format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg and run libcamera-still with "-o <filename> --width 640 --height 480 -q 85 --timeout 2000 --nopreview" (assume the images directory already exists), checking its return code and logging failures. Log all events, with timestamps, to /home/pi/motion_capture.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all libgpiod resources and closing file descriptors. Do not use wiringPi, and do not use ZeroMQ or any network publishing — save to the local file system only.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32-bit or 64-bit) that captures a single frame from a USB UVC camera at /dev/video0 using the V4L2 API, crops a specific region, and saves the result as a raw YUYV file — V4L2 only, no libgpiod, pigpio, or wiringPi. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to control two SG90 servo motors connected to GPIO17 (pan) and GPIO18 (tilt), forming a basic pan-tilt camera mount. Read user input from stdin — arrow keys for up, down, left, right — to adjust pan and tilt angles in 5-degree increments, enforcing limits of 0 to 180 degrees, with initial angles of 90 degrees (neutral). Use pigpio's hardware PWM at 50 Hz, with pulse widths ranging from 500 microseconds (0 degrees) to 2500 microseconds (180 degrees). Handle pigpio initialization failure gracefully by printing an error and exiting with code 1. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C) or a 'q' input, set both servos to the neutral position and terminate pigpio cleanly. Validate all angle inputs and PWM settings, printing clear error messages for out-of-range angles or PWM failures. Include a 100 ms delay between commands to prevent excessive CPU usage. Use only pigpio functions — not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that displays real-time CPU temperature, read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, and CPU usage percentage, computed from /proc/stat, on a 128x64 I2C OLED screen using the SSD1306 driver. Handle file read errors by returning specific error strings to the display instead of the missing values, and handle I2C communication failures by logging a message to stderr and exiting gracefully, checking every I2C write operation for an error return. Include signal handling for SIGINT so that all resources are released cleanly on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, using the pigpio library, that reads pulses from a YF-S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 and calculates the flow rate in liters per minute using the sensor's calibration figure of approximately 450 pulses per liter. Every 10 seconds, also update a small HD44780 LCD screen connected via I2C (bus 1, address 0x27) to display the current flow rate together with the accumulated volume, using pigpio's I2C functions and handling any I2C communication errors that occur. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library exclusively (no wiringPi) to display real-time wind speed and direction on a 16x2 LCD (PCF8574 I2C backpack at address 0x27, bus 1), updating every 500 ms. Count anemometer pulses on GPIO17 via a rising-edge interrupt, computing wind speed as pulses multiplied by 0.5 m/s per pulse, accumulated over each 500 ms sample window. Read the wind vane from channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0/CE0, mode 0, 1 MHz, linearly mapping the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to 0-359 degrees. Check every pigpio, I2C, and SPI call; detect sensor-absent conditions such as an ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023, or I2C/SPI failures, and print diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run. Use pigpio's I2C and SPI bit-bang helpers (bbI2COpen/bbSPIOpen) or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via pigpio's spi0SPIOpen/i2cOpen where appropriate. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all resources — the SPI handle, the I2C handle, and pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to measure water flow rate with a single YF-S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), using the sensor's calibration factor of 7.5 pulses per liter. Display the real-time flow rate on an LCD1602 display connected via I2C (bus 1, PCF8574 address 0x27), showing "Flow Rate:" on the first line and the value as "X.XX L/min" on the second line. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, GPIO mode and alert setup, I2C bus open and write failures, and sensor-absent paths such as zero pulses over an extended period. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program using the libgpiod library for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix. The matrix rows are anodes, connected via GPIO to +3.3V, and columns are cathodes, connected via GPIO to ground: rows on GPIO17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM numbering), columns on GPIO5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20. Implement a scanning display function that lights one row at a time — row HIGH and column LOW lights an LED (common-anode logic) — using a scan delay of 800 microseconds per row. Create two wave patterns, left-to-right and right-to-left, that shift each frame. Check all libgpiod calls, printing descriptive error messages to stderr and exiting with a non-zero code on failure. Handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing GPIO lines and cleaning up. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

Write a C program using the libgpiod v2 API (gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix with 8 row anodes and 8 column cathodes. Wire row pins GPIO2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 to the row anodes, and column pins GPIO14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 to the column cathodes through current-limiting resistors (e.g. 220 ohm). Scan columns from left to right with a 150 ms delay between columns: for each column, set the corresponding column cathode LOW and all row anodes HIGH to light the entire column, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW. Run the animation indefinitely until interrupted (Ctrl+C). Check every GPIO operation, handling chip-open failure, and cleanly release all GPIO lines on exit using a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

To achieve the task of reading distance data from a VL53L5CX ToF sensor using the Linux i2c-dev interface, we need to manually handle I2C communication. Below is a complete C program that accomplishes this task. The program initializes the sensor, reads the distance data from all 64 zones, and logs the results every 500 ms. It also includes robust error handling and resource release on all exit paths, including handling SIGINT.

```c

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a parking-assist system with a single HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor -- trigger on GPIO 23, echo on GPIO 24, both BCM -- and an SG90 servo controlled on GPIO 17 (BCM) that rotates between -90 degrees (closest, about a 1 ms pulse) and +90 degrees (farthest, about a 2 ms pulse) to indicate the measured distance. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to implement an interrupt-driven parking sensor with a single HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor on GPIO 17 (trigger, BCM) and GPIO 27 (echo, BCM), with a buzzer on GPIO 22 (BCM). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to control a gate with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x29 and an SG90 servo motor on GPIO18 (BCM, hardware PWM). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor: TRIG on GPIO 23 (physical pin 16, BCM, output, initially LOW) and ECHO on GPIO 24 (physical pin 18, BCM, input with a pull-down resistor). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for all GPIO, PWM, and I2C operations to implement a smart parking gate with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/SDA, GPIO3/SCL) at address 0x29 and a servo motor gate actuator. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control a gate actuator based on a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor connected via I2C bus 1 at address 0x29. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a single VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses libgpiod for GPIO control and the Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1 via ioctl), not wiringPi, to implement a proximity-based interactive art installation with a single MPR121 capacitive touch sensor at I2C address 0x5A. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24) and pan an SG90 servo (signal on GPIO18, hardware PWM-capable) to track it. #define SHT40_CRC8_POLYNOMIAL 0x31
#define SHT40_CRC8_INITIAL_VALUE 0xFF

static void sigint_handler(int sig) {
    gpioTerminate();
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);

static void calculate_crc8(const uint8_t *data, size_t length, uint8_t *crc) {
    *crc = SHT40_CRC8_INITIAL_VALUE;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        *crc ^= data[i];
        for (int j = 0; j < 8; j++) {
            if (*crc & 0x80) {
                *crc = (*crc << 1) ^ SHT40_CRC8_POLYNOMIAL;
            } else {
                *crc <<= 1;
            }
        }
    }

static void calculate_crc8(const uint8_t *data, size_t length, uint8_t *crc) {
    *crc = SHT40_CRC8_INITIAL_VALUE;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        *crc ^= data[i];
        for (int j = 0; j < 8; j++) {
            if (*crc & 0x80) {
                *crc = (*crc << 1) ^ SHT40_CRC8_POLYNOMIAL;
            } else {
                *crc <<= 1;
            }
        }
    }
}

    usleep(10000); // Wait at least 10 ms

    if (result != 6) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read from SHT40: %s\n", gpioErrmsg(result));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static void validate_crc8(const uint8_t *data, size_t length) {
    uint8_t crc = 0;
    calculate_crc8(data, length - 1, &crc);
    if (crc != data[length - 1]) {
        fprintf(stderr, "CRC8 checksum failed\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the standard Linux I2C i2c-dev interface to interface with a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Send the continuous measurement command (0x362F), wait for the conversion time of approximately 45 ms, and read 9 bytes containing pressure, temperature, and scale factor, each with an 8-bit CRC. Validate the CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial 0xFF) and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Convert the raw data to pressure in Pa and temperature in °C using the correct formulas. Log the timestamp, pressure, and temperature to a CSV file named 'airflow.csv' every 1 second. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM, ensuring the I2C file descriptor and any open file handles are properly closed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35-DIS-B sensor connected to I2C bus 1 at address 0x44 (ADDR pin tied to GND). Use the single-shot high-repeatability clock-stretching-disabled measurement command (0x2400); after sending it, wait at least 15 ms before reading 6 bytes (temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC, humidity MSB, humidity LSB, humidity CRC), validating both CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF). Convert raw values using T = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535 and RH = 100 * raw / 65535. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'environment.csv' (columns: timestamp,temperature_c,humidity_pct), writing a header row if the file does not already exist or is empty, sampling every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialisation, I2C open, every I2C read/write, CRC validation, and file open; on failure print a descriptive error to stderr and continue or exit appropriately. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) to periodically read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor at I2C address 0x40 on bus 1 (GPIO 2/3), simulating a greenhouse monitoring system. Use the Si7021's No Hold Master measurement commands (0xF5 for humidity, 0xF3 for temperature), polling with read attempts until data is available or a 100 ms timeout is reached; read 3 bytes (MSB, LSB, CRC) for each measurement and verify the CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0x00). Use the paired-reading command 0xE0 to read the temperature associated with the previous humidity measurement. Convert raw values using Temperature = 175.72 * raw / 65536.0 - 46.85 and Humidity = 125.0 * raw / 65536.0 - 6.0. Every 5 seconds, log to a CSV file named 'environment.log' with the header 'timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent' using ISO-8601 timestamps; on an I2C or CRC error, log a line with 'ERROR' in place of the values and print a descriptive message to stderr, but continue running. Check every system call return value, handle sensor-absent (I2C open failure or NACK) and bus-error paths, and if a read fails, reset the sensor by writing the reset command (0xFE) before the next cycle. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and exit gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a simplified HVAC airflow monitoring system. Use the continuous measurement command 0x362F, wait the specified conversion time, then read 9 bytes: pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC, and 3 scale factor bytes, validating CRC-8 for both the pressure and temperature raw values. Convert pressure using pressure = raw_pressure / scale_factor - 1000 (Pa), and temperature using temperature = raw_temperature / 200.0 - 45.0 (°C). Sample once per second and log each sample to 'airflow.dat' in binary format, with pressure and temperature each written as a float, keeping the file handle open across samples rather than reopening it on every write. Check pigpio initialisation, I2C open, command write, and read results, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use signal handling (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for a graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a DIY ventilation system. Send the continuous measurement command 0x3603, wait the conversion time of 45 ms, then read 9 bytes (3 words plus 3 CRC bytes), validating each CRC-8 using polynomial 0x31. Convert the raw pressure using the scale factor 60.0 to Pa. Log each reading with a timestamp to 'pressure_log.txt' every 5 seconds. Handle I2C write/read errors, CRC failures, and sensor-absent scenarios gracefully without crashing the program. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate pigpio cleanly before the process exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure from a Honeywell Zephyr HAF Series HAFBLF0100A2AX5 digital airflow sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x28, and drives a PWM fan on GPIO18 (a hardware-PWM-capable pin) at 25 kHz based on the computed flow rate. The sensor operates on the heat transfer principle and returns a 16-bit word whose 2 most significant bits are status bits; mask them off and shift the result right by 2 to obtain the 14-bit raw flow reading. Convert the 14-bit reading to flow rate using the linear transfer function where 1638 counts correspond to 0 SLPM and 14745 counts correspond to 10 SLPM. Scale the fan's PWM duty cycle linearly between 0% at 0 SLPM and 100% at 10 SLPM. Sample the sensor every 100 ms and log each reading with a timestamp to flow_log.txt in the comma-separated format "timestamp,pressure_Pa\n". Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, logging errors to stderr without crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: turn off the fan, close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read pressure and temperature from an STMicroelectronics LPS33HW sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x5D. On startup, read the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) and abort if it does not equal 0xB1. Configure CTRL_REG1 (0x10) to 0xB0 for block data update, 10 Hz output rate, and active mode. Read the 24-bit two's-complement pressure from PRESS_OUT_XL (0x28), PRESS_OUT_L (0x29), and PRESS_OUT_H (0x2A), storing it in an int32_t, and convert to hPa by dividing by 4096.0. Read the 16-bit two's-complement temperature from TEMP_OUT_L (0x2B) and TEMP_OUT_H (0x2C), storing it in an int16_t, and convert to Celsius using 42.5 + raw/480.0. Sample once per second using gpioDelay. Check the return value of every I2C read and write; on failure, write a timestamped error line to both stderr and the log file and continue the loop rather than exiting. Log each valid reading to environmental_data.txt, flushing after every write, in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX hPa, Temperature: XX.XX °C" using localtime_r for thread-safe timestamp formatting. Handle SIGINT with a volatile sig_atomic_t flag that exits the main loop, then close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read an STLM75 digital temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, reading temperature register 0x00 once per second. The STLM75 returns a 16-bit two's-complement word with 9-bit resolution (sign bit, 8 data bits, and the low 7 bits always 0); because pigpio's i2cReadWordData returns bytes in little-endian order, swap the two bytes before extracting the value, then right-shift by 7 and divide by 2 to get degrees Celsius. Store each reading in a 10-element circular buffer in memory and compute the running average. Turn on an LED on GPIO 17 when the average temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turn it off otherwise. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, and every I2C read; if a read fails, skip that iteration and continue. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so the program shuts down cleanly, turning off the LED, closing the I2C handle, and calling gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cClose, i2cReadDevice, i2cWriteDevice, gpioTerminate) to interface with a Sensirion SCD30 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x61. Set the measurement interval to 2 seconds and start continuous measurement with ambient pressure compensation disabled (0). Before each read, poll the data-ready flag with command 0x0202, then read the measurement with command 0x0300, returning 18 bytes (3 values of 4 data bytes plus 2 CRC bytes each). Implement the SCD30 CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) for every write command that carries arguments and verify the CRC on every value read. Log CO2 (ppm), temperature (°C), and humidity (%RH) with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps as comma-separated values to air_quality.log, flushing after each write, and drive a simulated ventilation system from the CO2 reading: OFF below 800 ppm, LOW between 800 and 1199 ppm, and HIGH at 1200 ppm or above. Handle every error path — pigpio initialization failure, I2C open/write/read failures, sensor non-response, data-not-ready, and CRC mismatches — by logging the error and continuing the loop rather than crashing. Use sigaction to catch SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop periodic measurement, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate(). In a mocked or emulated environment where the I2C hardware may be absent, initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, and if sensor initialization or reads fail, log the error and exit gracefully with code 0 rather than crashing or returning a nonzero status.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to periodically read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x21. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO 2, SCL on GPIO 3) at address 0x25. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64-bit kernel to periodically read temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC1000 sensor on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2 = SDA, GPIO 3 = SCL) at its default 7-bit address 0x40, using the Linux i2c-dev API (open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) rather than the deprecated wiringPi library. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Linux i2c-dev interface (open() and ioctl() on /dev/i2c-1) to periodically read pressure values from a Melexis MLX90819 (digital I2C version) sensor on I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x60. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from a Honeywell HIH6130 I2C sensor at address 0x27 on I2C bus 1. Convert the raw values using temperature = raw_T * 165.0/16383.0 - 40.0 and humidity = raw_H * 100.0/16383.0. Do not manipulate any GPIO pins for pull-up control; rely on the bus pull-ups. Sample every 5 seconds and log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a rolling file environmental_data.log, truncating it when it exceeds 1 MB. Check every I2C return code and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths robustly. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for GPIO timing to read pressure data from a Melexis MLX90824 SENT pressure sensor connected to GPIO 4 (BCM), for an automotive brake pressure monitoring system. Implement the SENT protocol with a tick time of 3 us: a synchronization pulse of 56 ticks, followed by a status nibble, 3 data nibbles, and a checksum nibble, where a valid nibble pulse width is 12 to 271 ticks (36-813 us). Validate the checksum as the sum of the nibbles modulo 16, and convert the 12-bit raw value to pressure using the linear transfer function raw * scale + offset. Detect sensor-absent (timeout) and bus-error (checksum or pulse-width) conditions, logging errors to stderr without crashing. Log each pressure reading with a timestamp to pressure_log.txt in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX Pa". Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean resource release.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to monitor a greenhouse with an Adafruit TMP117 High Precision Temperature Sensor over I2C bus 1 at the default address 0x48. On startup, verify the sensor's device ID register reads 0x0117. Read the temperature register 0x00 (2 bytes, signed, LSB = 0.0078125 °C) every 60 seconds and append each reading as a 4-byte little-endian float to a binary file named greenhouse_temps.dat. Handle I2C communication failures gracefully without crashing, and ensure clean resource release — the I2C handle, the file stream, and the pigpio library — on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT40 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x44, simulating a smart greenhouse environment monitor. Issue the high-precision measurement command 0xFD, wait at least 8.5 ms for the conversion, then read 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature, 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes humidity, 1 CRC byte. Validate both CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert the raw values using Temperature = -45 + 175 * (raw_temp / 65535.0) °C and Humidity = -6 + 125 * (raw_hum / 65535.0) %RH. Log each reading with a timestamp to environmental_data.txt in append mode, flushing after each write. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, the I2C write, the I2C read, and CRC validation, and handle file-operation errors as well. Handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the log file. Read the sensor every 5 seconds indefinitely.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to periodically sample temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP117 high-accuracy sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x48. Read the 2-byte big-endian temperature register 0x00 every 5 seconds and convert it using the 0.0078125 °C LSB resolution. Store readings in a rolling circular buffer in memory and persist the entire buffer to a binary file named temperature_log.dat on every sample and on exit. Check that pigpio initialization and I2C handle creation succeed. If a read fails, log the error, skip that sample, and continue running rather than crashing. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM that flushes the buffer to the file and releases all resources — the I2C handle and pigpio — on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHTC3 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x70, for an indoor air quality monitoring system. The SHTC3 operates at 1.8 V but tolerates 3.3 V on SDA/SCL; wire VDD to 3.3 V (Pin 1), VSS to GND (Pin 2), SDA to GPIO 2 (Pin 3), and SCL to GPIO 3 (Pin 4). Issue the normal-power measurement command 0x7866 (clock stretching disabled), wait at least 12.4 ms for the conversion, then read 6 bytes: temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC8, humidity MSB, humidity LSB, humidity CRC8. Validate each pair with CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert using T = 175 * raw / 65535 - 45 and RH = 100 * raw / 65535, rejecting readings outside -40 to 125 °C or 0 to 100 %RH. Log valid readings every 5 seconds to shtc3_environment.log in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,Temperature(C),Humidity(%)" with two decimal places, printing valid readings to stdout and errors to stderr. Handle I2C write/read errors, CRC failures, out-of-range values, and file-open errors gracefully without crashing. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, call gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a Bosch BMP280 pressure sensor over I2C-1 at address 0x76. Verify the chip ID equals 0x58 at register 0xD0 before proceeding, then read the 24-byte calibration block starting at 0x88 and apply the Bosch compensation formulas. Configure ctrl_meas (register 0xF4) for 1x oversampling on temperature and pressure in forced mode (0x27), triggering a measurement by writing the forced mode bits (0x01) each loop, and wait about 10 ms for conversion completion before reading 6 bytes of raw data from register 0xF7. Sample every 2 seconds and log timestamped pressure threshold breaches — above 1020 hPa or below 980 hPa — to pressure_log.txt. Handle I2C errors gracefully with up to 3 retry attempts that re-open the bus and re-verify the chip ID. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to shut down cleanly, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4B that logs temperature from a TMP117 sensor (I2C address 0x48, temperature register 0x00, 16-bit signed big-endian, LSB = 0.0078125 °C), humidity from an AHT20 sensor (I2C address 0x38, init command 0xBE 0x08 0x00, measure command 0xAC 0x33 0x00, 7-byte response with busy bit in data[0] bit 7, 20-bit humidity and temperature raw values), and motion detection from a PIR sensor on GPIO 17, into daily timestamped CSV files. Use libgpiod for GPIO access (gpiochip4, line 17, input direction) and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1) via ioctl for the sensors. Sample every 1 second, handle I2C errors with up to 3 retries and a 10 ms backoff, and check sensor presence at startup — print a warning but continue if a sensor is absent. Create a new log file each day at midnight with CSV header 'Timestamp,Temperature(C),Humidity(%),MotionDetected'. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Build with: gcc -o logger logger.c -lgpiod -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod library, through the Linux GPIO character-device interface, to monitor a YL-83 rain sensor connected on GPIO17, reading it as an active-low digital output where a value of 0 means rain has been detected, polling the line every 2 seconds. When rain is detected, close a window by driving an L298N motor driver board, with its enable line ENA on GPIO22, its first direction input IN1 on GPIO23, and its second direction input IN2 on GPIO24, so that the motor runs forward for 5 seconds and then stops. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, and explicitly handle the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened at startup. Ensure the motor is stopped and every requested GPIO line is released back to the system on program exit, whether that exit is triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM signal handling, and log each event with a timestamp to stdout. Do not include any DHT22 or humidity-sensing code in this program — the scope is limited strictly to the rain sensor and the motor control it drives.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library, and not wiringPi, to modulate a common-anode RGB LED, whose Red, Green, and Blue cathodes are wired to GPIO 17, 22, and 27 respectively, so that its color visually represents the current CPU load. Use hardware PWM through pigpio to control the brightness of each channel, clamping every PWM value to the 0-255 range. Map CPU load, computed by reading /proc/stat and comparing successive samples, onto a color gradient: 0% load renders Green (0,255,0), 50% load renders Yellow (255,255,0), and 100% load renders Red (255,0,0), sampling and updating every 500 ms. Handle any pigpio initialization failure by printing an error message to stderr and exiting with status code 1. Install handlers for both SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn the LED fully off, which for a common-anode LED means driving all channels to full off, and then cleanly call gpioTerminate() before the process exits. Do not include any temperature-sensor code in this program; the scope here is CPU load alone.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor over I2C-1 (SDA=GPIO2/pin3, SCL=GPIO3/pin5) at address 0x76, sending the data as a JSON string over UDP to 192.168.1.100:5000 every 5 seconds. Verify the chip ID equals 0x58 at register 0xD0 before proceeding, read the 24-byte calibration block at 0x88-0xA1, and apply the Bosch 64-bit compensation formulas. Use forced mode (write to register 0xF4) for low power, waiting for the measurement to complete before reading 6 bytes from register 0xF7. Handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor-absent paths, and UDP send failures gracefully. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, UDP socket, and pigpio library on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to dynamically control a PWM-driven cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM) based on temperature readings from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8). Initialize pigpio and open SPI channel 0 at 500 kHz, mode 0. Every 1 second, read the 32-bit MAX31855 register, extracting the signed 14-bit thermocouple temperature at 0.25°C resolution and checking the fault bit (bit 16) plus fault type bits OC (bit 0), SCG (bit 1), and SCV (bit 2). Drive the fan via hardware PWM on GPIO18 at 1 kHz with a 0-255 duty range, using a piecewise curve: 0% below 25°C, a linear ramp of 0-50 between 25-40°C, a steeper ramp of 50-200 between 40-60°C, and 100% above 60°C. Log each valid reading — timestamp, temperature, PWM duty cycle — into a 20-entry circular buffer. On SPI transfer errors or MAX31855 faults, print a diagnostic message to stderr and skip the fan update for that cycle. Handle SIGINT gracefully: stop PWM, close SPI, print the full buffer contents, and terminate pigpio before exiting. Check every pigpio call, including gpioInitialise, spiOpen, spiXfer, and gpioPWM.

Ensure clean resource release of file descriptors and file pointers on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Log timestamp, temperature, and duty cycle to fan_log.txt every 5 seconds. Handle file write errors, temperature read failures, and pigpio initialization failures gracefully. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor over I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA=GPIO2/pin3, SCL=GPIO3/pin5) and logs readings with timestamps to weather_data.txt in append mode, using only the Linux i2c-dev interface (no wiringPi, no pigpio). The default BMP280 address is 0x76 (SDO tied to GND); also try 0x77 as a fallback. The sensor is powered from the 3V3 rail, never 5V. Read chip_id from register 0xD0 and verify it equals 0x58, aborting with a clear error if it does not match, then read the 24-byte calibration block starting at register 0x88 (dig_T1..dig_P9) and apply the Bosch 64-bit compensation formulas. Configure ctrl_meas (register 0xF4) for forced mode with oversampling x1 for temperature and pressure, re-writing ctrl_meas each loop to trigger each measurement, and poll the status register (0xF3) bit 3 (measuring) until it clears, with a timeout, before reading 6 bytes of raw data from register 0xF7 (press_msb) and combining into 20-bit values. Log every 5 seconds in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa'. Check every I/O call — open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs — and handle failures gracefully. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to exit the loop cleanly, closing the I2C file descriptor and exiting 0. If the sensor disappears mid-run, log the error to stderr and attempt to continue or exit gracefully.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from an LM75 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x48 using the libgpiod library (never wiringPi). Read the 16-bit temperature register (0x00) every 1 second; the value arrives two's-complement, MSB first, left-shifted by 5 bits (bits [15:5] hold the temperature, bits [4:0] are always 0), so divide the signed 16-bit value by 256.0 to get degrees Celsius. Log each reading to an in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 60 samples and compute the running average. Trigger an LED on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) if the temperature exceeds 28.0°C, turning it off otherwise. Use a background thread with a mutex-protected circular buffer for data acquisition. Check every I2C read/write and GPIO init call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging to stderr and attempting re-initialization, and ensure clean resource release — close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, destroy the mutex — on all exit paths including SIGINT.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that regulates a resistive heater connected through a logic-level MOSFET on GPIO18 (hardware PWM) using the pigpio library (not wiringPi). Measure temperature with a PT100 RTD through a MAX31865 RTD-to-digital converter over SPI0 (CE0, SPI mode 1, 500 kHz), using a 430-ohm reference resistor for the PT100 (nominal resistance 100 ohms). Initialize the MAX31865 by writing 0xC1 to the configuration register (0x80) to enable VBIAS, enable auto-conversion, and clear faults. Read the 15-bit RTD code from registers 0x01 (MSB) and 0x02 (LSB), check the fault bit (D0 of MSB), and read the fault status register (0x07) to diagnose open, over-voltage, or under-voltage faults. Convert the RTD code to resistance using R_rtd = (code / 32768) * R_ref, then convert resistance to temperature using the Callendar-Van Dusen equation R = R0 * (1 + A*t + B*t^2), solved for t, for t >= 0. Run a PID control loop every 100 ms, outputting a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 at 1 kHz with pigpio range 1000 for 0-100% duty.
