prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to control a solid-state relay on GPIO17, modulating a resistive heater to maintain a target temperature read from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over the hardware SPI peripheral (SPI0, CE0: GPIO8 CS, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz. Log temperature and PWM duty cycle to heater_log.csv with ISO-8601 timestamps. Implement a PI controller with anti-windup and a safe maximum duty cycle of 80% to prevent overheating. On SPI read failure or a MAX31855 fault (open circuit, short to GND, or short to VCC), immediately set the heater duty cycle to 0%, log the error, and continue running. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown — turn off the heater, close SPI, close the log file, terminate pigpio. The target temperature defaults to 25.0°C. Do not include any network or socket code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to create a mood light that adjusts a common-anode RGB LED based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp every 0.5 seconds. Red, Green, and Blue cathodes connect to GPIO 17, 18, and 27 (BCM), with the common anode on 3.3 V and current-limiting resistors on each cathode line. Use hardware PWM via gpioPWM (range 0-255) on each pin; since the LED is common-anode, a channel is fully off at duty 255 and fully on at duty 0, so invert the desired brightness accordingly. Apply temperature thresholds from the millidegree sysfs value: below 40000 m°C, solid Blue (R=0,G=0,B=255); 40000-59999 m°C, solid Green (R=0,G=255,B=0); 60000 m°C and above, solid Red (R=255,G=0,B=0). Print the current temperature (m°C) and RGB values to stdout each cycle. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(); on failure, print an error to stderr and exit with non-zero status. When reading the temperature file, handle both fopen failure and short or failed reads (check ferror); on any read error, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip the update cycle rather than using a bogus value, and close the file handle on every code path. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM, using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and performing cleanup in main's exit path rather than inside the handler, so that Ctrl+C cleanly turns off all three channels (PWM duty 255 for common-anode off) and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting. Run an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), using the pigpio library for bit-banging the 1-wire protocol and libcurl for HTTP POST requests. Send a start signal by pulling the data line low for at least 1 ms, then read the 40-bit response. Parse the data, validate the 8-bit checksum, and POST the readings as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity. Handle sensor-absent, checksum, and network errors gracefully with up to 3 retries. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library that toggles data logging from a BMP180 pressure sensor (I2C address 0x77 on bus 1) to pressure_log.txt via a push-button interrupt on GPIO4, containing timestamped pressure readings in hPa. Use a falling-edge ISR on GPIO4 with an internal pull-up to toggle logging on and off, debouncing in the ISR using pigpio tick comparison (at least 200000 us). Read the BMP180 calibration coefficients from registers 0xAA-0xBE at startup and validate them, failing cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid data. Use oversampling OSS=3 for pressure measurements with the correct 26 ms conversion delay, and implement the full Bosch BMP180 compensation algorithm using integer arithmetic, with no floating-point pow calls. Log only when logging is enabled; when disabled, print a status message. Sample every 2 seconds. Handle SIGINT cleanly by closing the I2C handle and releasing pigpio resources before exiting. Check every I2C read/write return value and report errors to stderr.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity from a DHT22 sensor on BCM GPIO 4 (physical pin 7) and POSTs the humidity value as JSON to http://your-server.com/api/humidity using libcurl, using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for the timing-critical GPIO reads. Initialize pigpio with gpioInitialise() and check for errors, implement the DHT22 single-wire protocol with correct start-signal timing (pull the data line low for at least 1 ms, then high for 20-40 µs, then release), and read the 40-bit response with microsecond-level edge timing via gpioRead(). Validate the checksum and retry up to 3 times on sensor failure with a 2-second backoff. POST the humidity reading with Content-Type: application/json using libcurl, retrying up to 3 times on network or HTTP errors. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, calling gpioTerminate() and curl_global_cleanup() on all exit paths, and log to syslog. Include a command-line option -s <url> to override the default server URL. Read every 10 seconds in the main loop, handling all error paths: sensor absent, checksum failure, curl init failure, and non-2xx HTTP responses.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler through the sysfs thermal framework, using no third-party GPIO libraries. Read the CPU temperature (millidegrees Celsius) from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp every 5 seconds and write the fan state to /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state using a tiered speed map: below 45°C, state 0 (off); below 55°C, state 1; below 65°C, state 2; 65°C and above, state 3 (max). Validate the cooling device's max_state before writing, to ensure the requested state is within bounds. Check all file opens, reads, writes, and parses, and handle transient read failures by retrying on the next cycle. Log every fan speed change with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, but do not log when the speed has not changed. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT and SIGTERM: stop the fan (state 0), log the shutdown, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to implement a PID controller that maintains a target temperature by PWM-controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 (hardware PWM, 1 kHz carrier, 0-100% duty). Read temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over SPI0 (CLK=GPIO11, CS=GPIO8/CE0, DO=GPIO9) at 500 kHz, reading 4 bytes per sample. Log the temperature, PWM duty cycle, and PID output to heater_log.txt every second. Handle SPI communication errors and thermocouple faults — open circuit, short to GND, short to VCC — by parsing the MAX31855 fault bits, logging errors to the same file, disabling the heater, and resetting the PID state. Include a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100°C or falls below 0°C. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM: heater off, SPI closed, pigpio terminated. Use Kp=1.0, Ki=0.1, Kd=0.01, and target=50°C as defaults.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to modulate a 25 kHz PWM signal on GPIO18 (physical pin 12) to control a Noctua NF-A4x10 5V PWM fan, dynamically adjusting fan speed based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp (in millidegrees Celsius). Use a linear mapping: 0% duty at 40°C and below, 100% duty at 70°C and above, with linear interpolation in between. Log the timestamp, temperature (°C), and PWM duty cycle (as a 0-100 percentage) to a comma-separated file cooling_log.csv with a CSV header, polling the temperature every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialization, verify the PWM frequency and duty cycle calls, handle file I/O errors, and gracefully shut down on SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning off the fan and releasing resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1. Both sensors share the default I2C address 0x08, so assume they are connected through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout (or similar I2C hub) that maps them to addresses 0x08 and 0x09. Continuously poll both sensors every 1 second using the SLF3S-1300F continuous measurement command 0x3608, reading 3 bytes per sensor (2 data bytes plus 1 CRC byte) and validating the CRC-8 checksum, skipping the logging if the CRC fails. Convert readings using raw_value * 0.01 to get flow rate in ml/min. Log the flow rates to a comma-separated file named flow_log.txt (format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2). Handle I2C errors robustly with up to 3 retries per sensor. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, closing all I2C handles and terminating pigpio.

Develop a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to monitor a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall-Effect Latch sensors: Sensor A (Channel A) on GPIO17 and Sensor B (Channel B) on GPIO18. Since the TMAG5110A1 has an open-drain output, configure internal pull-up resistors on both pins. Implement a standard 2-bit quadrature state machine to track rotation increments over 360 pulses per revolution, logging every state change with a timestamp and the normalized angular position (0.00 to 360.00 degrees) to encoder_log.txt. Ensure robust error handling for GPIO initialization and file I/O, and implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM using pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod for GPIO and the Linux I2C character-device interface (linux/i2c-dev.h) to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default 7-bit address 0x39. Read the 16-bit red and IR channel data from the FIFO data register (0x60), handling I2C read/write errors and sensor-absent conditions. Trigger an LED on GPIO 17 (active-high) if the IR reading exceeds a threshold of 2000. Sample every 100 ms and log timestamped readings to adpd144ri_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp,red,ir). Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, cleanly releasing all resources — the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and log file — on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to read RPM from a Melexis MLX90254 magnetic speed sensor connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, configured as input with a pull-down), which outputs 1 pulse per revolution. Calculate RPM over a 1-second interval by counting rising edges only, and log RPM values with timestamps to rpm_log.txt in append mode, flushed immediately. Use a pthread mutex to protect the pulse counter between the ISR and the main thread. Check pigpio initialization, ISR registration, and log file opening. Use a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown that terminates pigpio, closes the log file, and destroys the mutex. If the sensor is absent (0 pulses), log 0.00 RPM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1) to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor at I2C address 0x39. Read the PART_ID register (0x00) to verify the sensor is present, then read the red and IR channel data from the FIFO data registers, handling I2C errors and sensor-absent paths robustly. Trigger an LED on GPIO 17 if the IR reading exceeds a threshold of 2000. Sample every 100 ms and log timestamped readings to adpd144ri_log.txt in CSV format. Clean up all resources — the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and log file — on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use the deprecated bcm2835 or wiringPi libraries.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod API (not sysfs or wiringPi) to sample the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier. Connect the MAX9814 OUT pin to GPIO 17 (configured as input) and the GAIN pin to GPIO 18 (configured as output), setting GPIO 18 LOW to select 60dB gain. Since the MAX9814 provides an analog signal, rapidly poll the digital input pin, at a 10 ms interval, to detect rising edges (logic HIGH) as peak sound events. Log each detected peak to audio_log.txt with a timestamp formatted as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL', where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge. Handle all libgpiod initialization and I/O errors robustly, checking the return value of every API call, and ensure clean release of all libgpiod resources on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Print a startup message and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to monitor flow rate from a Sensirion SLF3S-4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected on I2C bus 1 at the default 7-bit address 0x36, for a microfluidic drug delivery system. Initialize the sensor by sending the 2-byte command 0x3608 to start continuous measurement. Every 1000 ms, read 3 bytes from the sensor: a 16-bit raw flow value (MSB first) followed by a CRC-8 byte, and validate it using the Sensirion CRC-8 algorithm (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF); if the CRC check fails, log an error and skip that reading. Convert the raw 16-bit signed value to a flow rate in uL/min by dividing by 1000.0. Log each valid reading to a CSV file named 'flow_log.csv' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min', opening the file once at startup in append mode, keeping it open, and flushing after each write rather than reopening repeatedly. Check every pigpio initialization, I2C open, write, and read call; on an I2C read or write failure, log the error to stderr and attempt to recover on the next loop iteration. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with a Honeywell MICS-VZ-89TE VOC sensor connected on I2C bus 1 at address 0x70. Read the 7-byte sensor state starting at register 0x00, extracting TVOC (ppb) from bytes 1-2 and eCO2 (ppm) from bytes 5-6 (big-endian), and compute an IAQ index using the formula IAQ = clamp(100 - (TVOC / 10.0) - ((eCO2 - 400) / 50.0), 0, 100). Every 5 seconds, log a timestamped line with the IAQ, TVOC, and eCO2 values to 'air_quality_log.csv'. Check every I2C read and write return value, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions without crashing. Handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod v1 API to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, active-high): the sensor outputs HIGH while touched and LOW when released. Open gpiochip0 by name and request the line as input with the consumer label "ttp223_tamper". Poll the line every 100 ms using CLOCK_MONOTONIC. If the sensor remains continuously touched for more than 5 seconds, print an intrusion alert to stdout once per touch event (not repeatedly), and reset the timer when the sensor is released. Check every libgpiod call for failure and print strerror(errno) on error; if a sensor read fails mid-loop, print an error and exit with EXIT_FAILURE after cleanup. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing the line and closing the chip on all exit paths. Do not use sysfs or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to continuously sample audio data from the InvenSense INMP441 I2S MEMS microphone and log 16-bit PCM samples to a raw file named 'audio_capture.pcm'. The INMP441 outputs 24-bit data left-justified in a 32-bit frame; extract the 24-bit data and right-shift it to produce 16-bit PCM samples. Acquire the I2S data through the Linux ALSA subsystem (via /dev/snd/pcmC0D0c or the snd-pcm kernel interface). Use the libgpiod library to drive the microphone's L/R select pin on GPIO 17 to select the left channel. Handle I2S initialization, data acquisition, and file I/O errors robustly, and implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a SainSmart IR Flame Sensor Module (LM393 comparator, IR photodiode) connected to GPIO 4 (digital DO pin), which outputs LOW when a flame is detected and HIGH when no flame is present. Poll the sensor every 50 ms with 50 ms software debouncing. When a flame is detected, drive a PWM-controlled cooling fan on GPIO 18 using hardware PWM at 100 Hz, scaling the duty cycle from 0 to 80% based on flame duration using an exponential curve; turn the fan off immediately when no flame is detected. Log all events (system start, flame detected, flame ended, shutdown) with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'flame_log.txt'. Implement robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, verify every GPIO read, handle sensor-absent conditions with a timeout, and cleanly release all resources (stop PWM, reset pins, terminate pigpio) on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with a TI AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor via SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) at 1 MHz, mode 0, assuming the AWR1642 is pre-configured via the TI mmWave SDK to stream range-Doppler heatmap data over SPI. Initialize pigpio and open SPI0.0 at 1 MHz mode 0. Write a binary log file header containing a magic number 0x52444144, an 8-byte timestamp, and a configuration struct recording a start frequency of 77 GHz, end frequency of 79 GHz, 64 chirps, 256 samples, and a 100 ms frame period. In a loop, assert a GPIO hardware trigger on GPIO 23 to request a frame, wait for a data-ready interrupt on GPIO 24, then read 32768 bytes of heatmap data via SPI full-duplex transfer, logging each frame with a per-frame timestamp and frame number. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM gracefully by closing SPI, releasing GPIO, and closing the file. Check all return codes and handle memory allocation failures.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod library to poll a KY-026 Flame Sensor (digital output) connected to GPIO 20 every 100 milliseconds. Trigger an alert and log only state transitions (flame detected / flame cleared) with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps to 'flame_log.txt'. Include robust error handling: check all libgpiod and file I/O calls, handle the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with a Texas Instruments OPT3001 Ambient Light Sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x44. Configure the sensor for continuous conversion mode with a 100 ms conversion time and automatic full-scale range. Continuously read the 16-bit result register (0x00), unpack the exponent (bits 15-12) and mantissa (bits 11-0), and compute lux as 0.01 * 2^exponent * mantissa. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'light_data.txt'. Robustly handle I2C transaction failures and sensor-absent conditions by retrying or logging errors without crashing. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, ensuring the I2C bus handle, pigpio library, and any open file handles are properly released on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod v2.x API (gpiod_line_config, gpiod_line_settings, gpiod_request_config, gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_chip_request_lines, gpiod_line_request_get_value, etc.) to read the SainSmart IR Flame Detection Sensor Module's digital output connected to GPIO line 17 (DOUT, active-low: the line reads 0 when a flame is detected). Request the line as input with bias pulled up. Every 1 second, log the flame detection status to the console with a timestamp formatted as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS', printing 'Flame Detected: YES' for line value 0 and 'Flame Detected: NO' for line value 1. Check every libgpiod call and syscall, printing clear error messages to stderr. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully with a signal handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag to exit the main loop. Clean up all resources on every exit path: release the line request, close the chip, and free all config/settings objects. Compile with: gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o flame_detect flame_detect.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read a Keywish KY-033 3-Way Tracing Sensor with left, center, and right digital outputs connected to GPIO 17, GPIO 18, and GPIO 27 respectively. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and each gpioSetMode() call, printing an error message to stderr and exiting with a non-zero status on failure. Every 50 ms (using usleep(50000)), read all three GPIOs and print their values to the console in the format 'Left: %d, Center: %d, Right: %d'. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, terminating pigpio before exit, and ensure all exit paths properly release pigpio resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod library to read a TTP226 8-channel digital touch sensor configured for direct GPIO output, with its 8 channels connected to BCM GPIO pins 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9. Every 100 ms, log the state of each channel (0 or 1) to the console. Check the return values of all libgpiod calls (chip open, line requests, reads), print descriptive errors to stderr, and ensure all resources (lines, chips) are properly released on all exit paths. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to read a TTP226 8-channel digital touch sensor whose OUT1-OUT8 pins are connected to Broadcom GPIO pins 2-9. Initialize pigpio and verify success, exiting with an error message on failure. Configure each GPIO as input with a pull-down resistor, validating each gpioSetMode/gpioSetPullUpDown call and aborting with a diagnostic if any fails. Every 100 ms (using gpioDelay(100000)), poll and log the state (0 = not touched, 1 = touched) of all 8 channels, printing a single timestamped line per sample in the format '[+1234 ms] CH1=0 CH2=1 ... CH8=0'. Install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so the sampling loop exits cleanly and gpioTerminate() is always called.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to read two Texas Instruments TMAG5110 Hall-Effect Latch sensors whose open-drain digital OUT pins are connected to BCM GPIO 4 and BCM GPIO 5, assuming external pull-up resistors so an unasserted output reads HIGH and an asserted (magnet-detected) output reads LOW. Every 500 ms, log the state of each sensor (HIGH/LOW) to the console. Verify pigpio initialization and GPIO mode configuration, handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for clean resource release, and ensure pigpio is properly terminated on all exit paths. Compile with: gcc -Wall -o hall_effect hall_effect.c -lpigpio -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the libgpiod library to periodically read an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor array whose outputs are connected to GPIO lines 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, and 9 (physical pins 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 15, 19, and 21). Configure each line as input with bias disabled. Poll all 8 channels every 50 ms and log the binary state of each channel to the console in CSV format with an ISO-8601 timestamp, one line per poll cycle, running until interrupted. Check every libgpiod call for failure, handle the case where the gpiochip cannot be opened or lines cannot be requested, and ensure all resources (line requests, chip) are properly released on all exit paths. Install a SIGINT handler for graceful shutdown on Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to poll an Omron D7E-1 tilt sensor connected to GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, BCM numbering), configured as a digital input with the internal pull-up resistor enabled. Poll the sensor every 100 ms and log a timestamped message to the console whenever the tilt state changes: print 'Tilted' when the input reads LOW (0) and 'Not Tilted' when it reads HIGH (1). Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and exit with an error message on failure; validate the GPIO read result and handle unexpected errors. Install a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) handler so the program exits cleanly and always calls gpioTerminate() on every exit path. Flush stdout after each log line so output is not lost on early termination, and print a startup banner before entering the poll loop.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1145 UV Index and Ambient Light sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x60. During initialization, verify the sensor's PART ID (0x45), write 0x17 to the HW_KEY register, configure the CHLIST register (0x01) to enable UV and ALS_VIS, and use the ALS_FORCE command (0x06) to trigger measurements. Every 1 second, continuously read UV index and Visible ALS data, print the readings to the console, and log them to a CSV file named 'uv_als_log.csv' with columns timestamp, uv_index, als_visible. Handle potential I2C errors and sensor-absent/bus-error paths gracefully. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to read flow rates from two Sensirion SLF3S-0600F Liquid Flow Sensors on I2C at addresses 0x36 and 0x37, using the Linux I2C character-device API (open()/ioctl() on /dev/i2c-1) for I2C communication and the libgpiod library for GPIO control. Initialize each sensor by sending the start-measurement command 0x3608 to I2C command register 0x08 and wait 100 ms for the first measurement. Read 9 bytes from register 0x00 (three 3-byte measurements: flow, temperature, CRC), validating each flow measurement with the Sensirion 8-bit CRC (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF); on an I2C error or CRC failure, log the error and skip that sensor's reading for the cycle. Convert the raw 16-bit signed flow value to ml/min using a scale factor of 0.036. Every 1 second, log the average flow rate of the two sensors to 'flow_log.txt', and drive an alarm on GPIO 17 high when that average is below 0.5 ml/min and low otherwise. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: release the GPIO lines, close the I2C file descriptors, and close the log file. Loop continuously with a 1-second interval between reads.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to poll a KY-033 Obstacle Avoidance Sensor Module connected to GPIO 4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), which outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its threshold and HIGH (1) otherwise. Initialize pigpio and verify success, printing an error to stderr and returning non-zero on failure. Configure GPIO 4 as input with the internal pull-up resistor enabled and poll it every 50 ms. On each detection (reading == 0), record a timestamp and the reading into a circular buffer of 100 entries that overwrites the oldest entry when full, and print an alert to stdout. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), print the entire buffer contents in chronological order with human-readable timestamps, release all pigpio resources, and exit cleanly. Do not use any deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit Bookworm) that interfaces with an Omron D7S vibration sensor over I2C (up to 400 kHz, default 7-bit address 0x55) using the Linux I2C character-device API (open()/ioctl(I2C_SLAVE)/read()/write() on /dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) to detect subtle vibrations indicating pre-failure in a small cooling fan. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x10 to register 0x1D (MODE_CONTROL) to switch it from standby to active mode, then wait until the operating-status register (0x1B) bit 0 reads 1; if the sensor does not become active within 1 second, print an error and exit. Every 500 ms, read the 16-bit signed acceleration registers X (0x2A/0x2B), Y (0x2C/0x2D), and Z (0x2E/0x2F), little-endian with LSB first, and convert the raw values to g using the scaling factor 0.0009765625 g/LSB. Log each sample as a CSV row with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'fan_health.csv' in append mode, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Check every I2C syscall return value; on a read/write/ioctl failure, print a diagnostic to stderr and retry on the next iteration rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file, then exit. The program should run until interrupted by the user.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with two Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors (active-LOW outputs, logic 0 = obstacle detected) connected to GPIO 23 (Sensor 1 OUT) and GPIO 24 (Sensor 2 OUT), triggering an LED on GPIO 25 (through a 220-330 ohm resistor to GND) when an obstacle is detected within approximately 10 cm of either sensor. Poll both sensors every 100 ms. Turn the LED ON immediately when either sensor reads LOW, and turn it OFF when both read HIGH. Verify pigpio initialization, validate every gpioSetMode/gpioRead/gpioWrite return code, and ensure clean resource release (gpioTerminate) on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a conveyor belt with two E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensors connected to GPIO 17 and GPIO 18, which output LOW (0) when an object is detected and HIGH (1) when clear. A stall is confirmed when both sensors read LOW continuously for at least 2 seconds; on a confirmed stall, log a timestamped entry to 'stall_log.txt', avoiding duplicate log entries for the same stall event. Check pigpio initialization, validate every sensor read, handle file I/O errors, and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with a Texas Instruments TMAG5170-Q1 I2C 3D Hall-Effect sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x0E (A0=A1=0). Configure the sensor for continuous-conversion mode with all three axes enabled and a 50 mT range. Verify the device ID register (0x00, expected value 0x8D) at startup, and write a CSV header row to 'magnetic_log.csv' if the file is newly created. Every 100 ms, read the X, Y, and Z magnetic field readings, convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to mT using the appropriate LSB scale factor for the 50 mT range, and log them with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'magnetic_log.csv'. Check every I2C read/write return code, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging errors to stderr and continuing. Register a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean resource release (close the I2C handle, close the file, call gpioTerminate). Run an infinite loop until interrupted by Ctrl+C.

Write a robust C daemon for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor a SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to GPIO 23, using a pull-down resistor on the input to avoid floating states when the sensor is dry. Poll the sensor every 2 seconds. When water is detected (logic HIGH), print an alert message to stdout and append a timestamped entry in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected' to 'flood_log.txt'. Check pigpio initialization, handle GPIO read failures with an automatic re-initialization attempt after 60 seconds (logging error entries to the same log file), and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (Bookworm or later) using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall-effect sensor via GPIO interrupts. The sensor output is connected to physical pin 7 (Broadcom GPIO 4), configured as input with the internal pull-up resistor enabled. Count rising-edge pulses in a 1-second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, and compute RPM as pulses_per_second * 60, assuming one pulse per revolution. Every 1-second sample, log 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>' to 'rpm_log.txt' (flushing the file after each write) and print it to stdout, logging RPM 0 rather than aborting when the sensor is absent or not rotating. Check every pigpio call and file-open call for errors and exit with a diagnostic message on failure. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers so Ctrl+C stops cleanly: disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to detect direction of rotation from two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall-effect sensors connected to GPIO 17 (Sensor A) and GPIO 27 (Sensor B) via hardware pull-up resistors, physically offset by 90 degrees to produce a quadrature signal. Use pigpio alerts (gpioSetAlertFunc) for edge-triggered interrupts instead of polling, and implement a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to determine direction, protecting the shared state between the ISR and main loop with a mutex. Log each detected rotation event (CW or CCW) with a millisecond-precision timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm) to 'rotation_log.txt'. Check all error paths: gpioInitialise(), gpioSetAlertFunc(), gpioSetPullUpDown(), and file open. Use a signal handler (SIGINT/SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, ensuring the log file is flushed/closed and pigpio is terminated. The main loop should wait on a condition variable or sleep, not busy-spin. Never use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library's line request API to interface with a SainSmart TTP223B digital capacitive touch sensor whose OUT pin is connected to GPIO 23 (physical pin 16), and an LED on GPIO 18 (physical pin 12) with a current-limiting resistor. Poll the touch sensor every 50 ms (to avoid busy-waiting) and illuminate the LED only while the sensor is actively touched. Check all libgpiod calls, including chip opening, line requests, reads, and writes, handling the case where the GPIO chip is unavailable. Log all touch events, errors, and startup/shutdown messages to the system syslog using openlog/syslog. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers to ensure the LED is turned off and resources are released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library's line event interface to read touch input from a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), which outputs HIGH (3.3 V) when touched and LOW when idle. On each rising-edge touch detection (with approximately 50 ms software debounce), toggle an LED connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12). Initialize the LED line as output and drive it LOW at startup. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line request, event wait, read, write) and print meaningful messages to stderr on failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully: release all libgpiod resources (lines and chip) and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with two SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensors (active-high) on GPIO 4 and GPIO 17, each controlling a distinct LED on GPIO 27 and GPIO 22 respectively, lit while the corresponding sensor is touched. Use a 50 ms polling loop for debounce. Log every touch and release event (sensor pin, Unix timestamp, and new state) into a 100-entry circular buffer in RAM with an overflow counter tracking how many events were overwritten once the buffer wraps. Check the return value of gpioInitialise and every gpioSetMode/gpioWrite/gpioRead call, printing a diagnostic to stderr on any failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, turning off both LEDs and calling gpioTerminate before exiting. On shutdown, print the full log buffer contents and the overflow count to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a Raindrop Sensor Module (digital output, active-low: reads LOW (0) when rain is detected, HIGH (1) when dry) connected to GPIO 17, with the internal pull-up resistor enabled so the input is defined when the sensor is disconnected. Poll the sensor every 500 ms and log only state transitions, writing timestamped 'Rain Detected' or 'No Rain' messages to /var/log/rain_events.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the log file and releasing pigpio resources on all exit paths. Check the return value of every pigpio call and of fopen.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to monitor a rotating shaft's RPM using two DRV5032FJDBZR Hall-Effect sensors (push-pull outputs, 3.3 V) connected to GPIO 17 and GPIO 18. Implement a debounce mechanism (approximately 5 ms) to avoid false readings, and calculate and print the RPM to the console assuming 2 pulses per revolution. Log timestamps and sensor state changes to a CSV file named 'shaft_log.txt' in the format 'timestamp,sensor1_state,sensor2_state'. Handle potential GPIO initialization and file I/O errors gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C). Include all required standard headers (e.g., errno.h, string.h) so the code compiles cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read heart rate and SpO2 data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 I2C-based optical sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x28. Initialize pigpio, open the I2C bus, and verify the sensor is present by reading the PART_ID register at 0x00. Configure the sensor for continuous measurement by writing to the CONFIG register at 0x30. Once per second, read heart rate data from register 0x02 and SpO2 data from register 0x04, and log each reading with a timestamp in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Heart Rate: X BPM, SpO2: Y%%' to 'biometric_log.txt' in append mode, flushing after each write. Check every I2C read/write return value and handle failures; on communication errors, print a message to stderr and continue the loop. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and log file and terminating pigpio before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor structural integrity of a miniature bridge model using two digital tilt sensors, which output HIGH when tilted beyond their threshold, connected to GPIO 17 (sensor 1) and GPIO 18 (sensor 2), both configured as inputs with internal pull-down resistors enabled. Connect an active-high alarm (buzzer/LED) to GPIO 27, initialized LOW. Poll at a 100 ms interval using gpioDelay. If either sensor reads HIGH continuously for more than 2 seconds, activate the alarm (GPIO 27 HIGH); when both sensors return to LOW, deactivate the alarm. Log all tilt-start, threshold-exceeded, and tilt-end events with ISO-8601 timestamps (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS) to 'bridge_integrity.log'. Check pigpio initialization, log file opening, and gpioRead return values. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown (deactivate the alarm, close the log file, call gpioTerminate), ensuring the alarm is deactivated on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to interface with an Omron D7S-A0011 seismic sensor over I2C bus 1 (default 7-bit address 0x1D, SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3). Initialize the sensor by verifying its presence and clearing the power-down bit in CTRL1 (register 0x1F). Every 100 ms, poll the 3-axis acceleration registers (0x28-0x2D, little-endian, 6-byte block read) and compute the Euclidean vibration magnitude; if it exceeds a threshold of 500, turn on an LED on GPIO 17 for 1 second, then turn it off. Log every threshold-exceeding event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the peak vibration value to 'seismic_events.log'. Handle I2C communication errors and sensor-absent conditions gracefully with up to 3 retries per read. Ensure all resources (I2C handle, pigpio library, log file) are released cleanly on Ctrl+C/SIGINT. Build with: gcc -O2 -Wall -o seismic seismic.c -lpigpio -lm -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod library to read obstacle detection data from four Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance Sensors whose OUT pins are connected to GPIO 4, 17, 27, and 22 (active-low: 0 = object detected). If any sensor detects an object, turn ON an LED connected to GPIO 18; otherwise turn it OFF. Poll the lines every 50 ms. Robustly handle GPIO initialization errors (e.g., chip open, line request failures) and cleanly release all resources on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use blocking delays that would prevent prompt signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod (v1.6+) to monitor 5 Keyes KY-026 flame sensors on BCM GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, and 27 (physical pins 3, 5, 7, 11, 13), wiring each sensor's digital output (LOW when a flame is detected, HIGH otherwise) to its GPIO and VCC/GND to 3.3V and GND. Poll all five lines once per second. On a rising-edge transition from no-flame to flame, confirmed by a 50 ms debounce re-read, append an event line to /var/log/flame_events.log formatted as '<ISO 8601 UTC timestamp> - Sensor ID: <id> (GPIO <pin>) - Flame Detected'. Use syslog (facility LOG_USER, ident 'flame_monitor') for startup, read-error, and shutdown messages. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line get, line request, line read) and every file I/O call (fopen, flock, fprintf, fflush); log and continue on per-sensor read failures rather than aborting, aborting only if chip open or line acquisition/request fails. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, release all requested lines, close the chip, and call closelog() on both normal and error paths. Track individual line pointers in an array rather than using gpiod_line_bulk_* APIs. Compile with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o flame_monitor flame_monitor.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod v1.x API to read the 8 individual touch states from a TTP226 8-channel capacitive touch sensor whose outputs OUT0-OUT7 are connected to BCM GPIO pins 5, 6, 13, 19, 26, 12, 16, and 20 respectively. Poll all eight pins every 50 milliseconds, logging only state changes (touch detected / released) to the console with ISO-8601 timestamps and the sensor index plus BCM pin number. Implement robust error handling for GPIO chip initialization, line resolution, bulk line requests, and read failures, printing a descriptive error (including errno) and exiting with a non-zero status on unrecoverable failures. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C). The code must compile cleanly with gcc -Wall -Wextra -lgpiod and must not rely on libgpiod v2-only APIs such as struct gpiod_line_bulk.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to implement an adaptive grow light system with a VEML7700 lux sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x10. Configure the sensor with ALS gain 1/8 (0x00) and ALS integration time 100 ms (0x00) by writing a 16-bit value to config register 0x00 (little-endian: low byte first, high byte second). Read ambient light from ALS register 0x04 (16-bit little-endian) once per second and convert it to lux using lux = raw * 0.0576. Control an LED on GPIO 18 via hardware PWM at 1000 Hz with range 0-100, using adaptive brightness logic: lux < 100 -> 100%, lux < 500 -> 75%, lux < 1000 -> 50%, lux >= 1000 -> 25%. Log each sample to 'grow_log.txt' with an ISO timestamp, lux value, brightness, and error code, flushing after each write. Check pigpio initialization, I2C open, sensor config write, ALS read, and PWM operations; log and handle sensor-absent/bus-error paths. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, turn off the LED, close I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library for a simulated security keypad that interfaces with an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module whose 8 digital output channels are connected to GPIO 2-9 (BCM numbering), and an LED on GPIO 17 that lights whenever any touch is detected. Initialize pigpio and verify success, exiting with an error message on failure; configure GPIO 2-9 as inputs with pull-down resistors and GPIO 17 as an output. Poll the inputs every 50 ms and debounce each channel so a single touch is logged only once per press. Log each new touch event to 'touch_log.txt' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS - Channel X Touched', where X (1-8) corresponds to GPIO 2-9. Turn the LED on when any channel transitions from untouched to touched, and off when all channels are released. Check all file I/O operations for errors and print diagnostics to stderr. Implement a clean signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turns off the LED, releases pigpio resources, and exits gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read ambient light data from a Texas Instruments OPT3001 sensor for a smart greenhouse environment monitoring system. Use I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, pigpio bus 1), OPT3001 address 0x44, configuration register 0x01, and result register 0x00. Configure the sensor for continuous conversion mode with automatic full-scale range and a 100 ms conversion time using configuration word 0xC810; pigpio's i2cReadWordData/i2cWriteWordData use little-endian word order while the OPT3001 expects/reports big-endian (MSB first), so byte-swap the 16-bit values before writing and after reading. After writing the configuration, wait at least 100 ms for the first conversion before reading the result register. Once per second, read the 16-bit result register, where bits 15-12 are the exponent and bits 11-0 are the mantissa, and compute lux = mantissa * 0.01 * (2^exponent). Log each reading to 'light_data.txt' as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, <lux_value>' with two decimal places, and also print the lux value to stdout for live monitoring. Check the return value of every pigpio and file I/O call; if i2cOpen or i2cReadWordData fails, print a descriptive error to stderr and skip that iteration, or exit gracefully on init failure. Install a SIGINT handler for clean shutdown: close the I2C handle and call gpioTerminate(). Ensure the log file is flushed and closed properly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a KY-026 Flame Sensor whose digital output (DO) is connected to GPIO 4 (BCM), outputting LOW (0) when a flame is detected and HIGH (1) otherwise. Poll the sensor every 500 milliseconds and log every reading with a timestamp to 'fire_events.log' (append mode). When a flame is detected (LOW), trigger an alert by setting GPIO 17 (BCM) HIGH for 1 second, then LOW. Check pigpio initialization, log file opening, and every GPIO read/write call; handle sensor read failures by logging the error and continuing. Ensure clean resource release (close the log file, reset GPIO, terminate pigpio) on all exit paths, including SIGINT (Ctrl+C), using signal-safe cleanup and avoiding unsafe functions in signal handlers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library to read capacitive touch events from a TTP223 touch sensor connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7), configured as an input with a pull-down bias. Poll the line with a debounce interval of approximately 50 ms, and on every press or release transition append a line to the text file 'touch_log.txt' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Detected' or 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Released', flushing the file after each write. Verify every libgpiod call and print a diagnostic to stderr on failure; if the log file cannot be opened, release all GPIO resources before exiting with a non-zero status. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by releasing the line, closing the chip, closing the log file, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to monitor coolant flow in a miniature liquid cooling system with a Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL), address 0x08. To start continuous measurement, send the 2-byte command sequence 0x36, 0x08 (0x3608) and wait at least 2 ms before the first read. Each read must fetch exactly 3 bytes: a big-endian signed 16-bit raw flow value followed by a CRC-8 byte (polynomial 0x31, init 0xFF); validate the CRC and flag the reading as an error on failure. Convert the raw value to ml/min using raw / 90.0, sampling once per second. Log the flow rate, raw sensor flags, and a computed status string to a comma-separated 'cooling_log.csv', writing the header row 'Timestamp,Flow Rate (ml/min),Status' only when the file is newly created. Check every pigpio, I2C, and file operation for errors; on an I2C read failure or CRC failure, log the row with status ERROR and attempt recovery by re-initializing the I2C handle. Validate the converted flow rate against a plausible range of 0.0 to 100.0 ml/min, logging out-of-range values with status INVALID. Handle SIGINT for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, closing the file, and terminating pigpio on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to poll three KY-033 obstacle-avoidance sensors (IR reflective, digital output) wired to GPIO17 (left), GPIO27 (middle), and GPIO22 (right). Poll all three lines every 50 ms and append each reading (0 or 1 per sensor) with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'path_log.csv' with columns timestamp,left,middle,right. Verify that the gpiochip opens successfully, that each line can be requested as input, and that file I/O succeeds. Handle SIGINT cleanly by releasing all GPIO lines, closing the chip, flushing, and closing the log file before exiting. Include the necessary system headers, such as errno.h and stdbool.h, so the code compiles without warnings under gcc -Wall -Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not pigpio or wiringPi) to monitor a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor (digital output, active-low: 0 = flame detected, 1 = no flame) connected to GPIO4 (BCM). Use edge-based event polling on the falling edge for efficient detection. When a flame is detected, print an alert with a timestamp to stdout and log the event, with its timestamp, to 'flame_events.txt'. Verify that the libgpiod chip and line requests succeed, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not sysfs, not wiringPi) to interface with a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO23 (BCM 23, input, active-high) and toggle an LED on GPIO24 (BCM 24, output). Use libgpiod line events on the rising edge (touch detected) with a 1-second poll timeout, toggling the LED on each event; debounce is not required since the TTP223 has built-in hardware debouncing. Log every touch event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the new LED state to 'touch_log.txt'. Open GPIO chip /dev/gpiochip4; if it cannot be opened or its lines cannot be requested, exit with an error after cleaning up any partially initialized resources. Check every libgpiod call and file operation for errors and report failures to stderr; if the log file cannot be opened, exit with an error. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod character-device API (gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_chip_get_line, gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value on device 'gpiochip0'; not wiringPi or sysfs) to implement a flame-detection safety system with a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor and an active buzzer. The KY-026 digital-output pin is connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11) and is active-low: it reads LOW when a flame is detected and HIGH otherwise. An active buzzer is connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) and sounds when its control line is driven HIGH. Poll the flame sensor every 500 ms. On a HIGH-to-LOW transition (software edge detection, not continuously while the line stays LOW), log the event with a timestamp to 'alert_log.txt' and activate the buzzer for 2 seconds, then continue. Log a 'System started' entry at startup and a 'System stopped' entry on clean shutdown. Break the 2-second buzzer activation and the 500 ms poll interval into 100 ms slices so the program can respond promptly to shutdown signals. Check every libgpiod call, file operation, and syscall for failure, printing a diagnostic via strerror(errno) to stderr and exiting non-zero if initialization fails. Include the headers errno.h, string.h, time.h, signal.h, unistd.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, and gpiod.h. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: turn the buzzer off, release the lines, close the chip, close the log file, and exit cleanly with code 0. Build with: gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o flame_alert flame_alert.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7) and toggle an LED on GPIO17 (physical pin 11). The TTP223B outputs HIGH (3.3 V) when touched and LOW when released. Configure GPIO4 as input and GPIO17 as output, checking all return values and reporting errors to stderr. Poll GPIO4 every 10 ms; on a rising edge (LOW-to-HIGH transition, not just level), toggle the LED and append a UTC ISO-8601 timestamped line to 'touch_log.txt'. Implement a 200 ms software debounce so a single touch does not register multiple events. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by turning off the LED, closing the log file, and calling gpioTerminate(). If the log file cannot be opened, print an error and exit non-zero; if a write to it fails, print a warning to stderr but continue running.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to interface with three Texas Instruments TMAG5110A1 Hall-effect latch magnetic sensors on GPIO4, GPIO17, and GPIO27 (BCM numbering). Each sensor's open-drain OUT pin drives a GPIO input with an internal pull-up enabled: it pulls low when a south pole is present and releases high otherwise, so a logic low means magnet-present and a logic high means magnet-removed. Initialize pigpio and verify every GPIO mode and pull call returns 0. Poll all three sensors every 100 ms using gpioDelay, and on the first read record the initial state without falsely logging a transition. Log each state change, with an ISO-8601 timestamp and sensor identifier, to 'magnet_log.txt'. Handle sensor read errors gracefully by logging to stderr and continuing. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for clean shutdown that close the log file and call gpioTerminate(). Include comments explaining the latch behavior.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read heart-rate data from a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GM optical heart-rate sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x4A. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, checking every return code. Verify the sensor's PART_ID register (0x00) reads 0x02 and HW_REV register (0x01) reads 0x01, aborting with a clear error if the sensor is absent or wrong. Configure the sensor by writing the LED current (0x3F), averaging (0x04), and enable (0x01) registers, checking each write. Read the 16-bit heart-rate register (0x2A) once per second using i2cReadWordData and convert the raw value to BPM using raw * 0.5. Apply a 5-sample moving average and validate that the filtered BPM is between 30 and 220 before logging. Append valid readings as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,BPM' to heart_rate.csv with an immediate flush. Retry on transient I2C read errors without crashing, and implement robust error handling for sensor-absent and bus-error conditions throughout. Handle SIGINT gracefully, closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (never wiringPi) to monitor a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor whose digital-output pin is connected to GPIO17 (Broadcom pin 17, physical pin 11). The sensor's DO pin is active-low: it reads LOW when flame is detected and HIGH when clear. Configure the line as input with an internal pull-up and poll it every 100 ms. When a falling edge is detected (HIGH-to-LOW transition, edge-triggered rather than level-triggered, to avoid duplicate alerts while the signal remains LOW), print 'FLAME DETECTED' to the console and append a line with the current timestamp and 'FLAME DETECTED' to 'flame_log.txt' in append mode, flushing immediately. Check every libgpiod call and file operation, and handle the case where the GPIO chip or line is unavailable. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown that releases the GPIO line, closes the chip, and closes the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the libgpiod v2+ bulk/config API (not sysfs, not wiringPi, not the deprecated libgpiod v1 simple API: gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_line_config_new, gpiod_line_settings_new, gpiod_line_settings_set_direction, gpiod_line_config_add_line_settings, gpiod_chip_request_lines, gpiod_line_request_get_value, gpiod_line_request_set_value, gpiod_line_request_release) to read an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module and display an 8-bit binary counter on GPIO outputs. Connect TTP226 outputs OUT1-OUT8, each active-high (3.3 V touched, 0 V idle), to GPIO 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 respectively (BCM numbering), and drive the counter display on GPIO17 (bit 0, LSB) through GPIO24 (bit 7, MSB). Poll the sensor lines every 10 ms, tracking each line's previous state to detect rising edges (inactive-to-active) without double-counting while held; on each new touch, increment an 8-bit counter that wraps 255 to 0 and immediately update the 8 output GPIOs so bit b appears on GPIO 17+b. Log every touch event to 'touch_log.txt' in append mode as 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ, Channel: <1-8>, Counter: <0-255>' and also print 'Touch on channel <N> | Counter: <V>' to stdout. Include a 200 ms stabilization delay after requesting lines before entering the main loop. Check every libgpiod call, file open, and I/O operation, reporting errors with strerror(errno); if gpiod_chip_open fails, print an error and exit non-zero; if any line-request call fails, release everything acquired so far and exit non-zero; if a sensor read errors, log to stderr and skip that channel without crashing; if an output write fails, log to stderr and continue; if the log file cannot be opened, log a warning to stderr and continue with stdout output. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by resetting all output pins to 0, releasing all libgpiod resources, closing the chip, and exiting cleanly with status 0. Build with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o touch_counter touch_counter.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not pigpio or wiringPi) to interface with a Keywish KY-033 4-Way Infrared Tracking Module whose four digital OUT pins connect to BCM GPIO 17, 18, 27, and 22. Each sensor output is active-low, where 0 means a line or surface is detected and 1 means none is detected. Use the modern libgpiod API (gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_get_value) to poll all four sensors every 100 ms and append a row to a timestamped CSV file named 'tracking_log.csv' with columns timestamp, sensor1, sensor2, sensor3, sensor4, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Robustly check every initialization and read call; if a GPIO request or read fails, print a clear error to stderr and continue if possible. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the CSV file, and flush the file after each write so data is not lost on abrupt termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod API (not sysfs, not wiringPi) to monitor two Omron D7E-5 tilt sensors connected to GPIO lines 17 and 18 (BCM numbering, physical pins 11 and 12). Configure both lines as inputs with an active-low pull-up (BiasPullUp) so an unconnected sensor reads high and a tilt event pulls the line low. Poll both lines every 100 ms and use edge detection with a 50 ms debounce window to avoid duplicate logs. When a line transitions from inactive (1) to active (0), log a timestamped event to /var/log/tilt_events.log in the exact format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Sensor X tilted\n', where X is 1 for GPIO17 and 2 for GPIO18. Handle chip-open failure, line-request failure, and read errors by printing a message to stderr and exiting or continuing gracefully. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that release all libgpiod resources (chip and lines) and close the log file cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (v2.x API, no sysfs, no wiringPi) to read digital reflectance data from two TCRT5000 IR obstacle-avoidance sensor modules on GPIO17 and GPIO27, each active-low (0 = obstacle detected, 1 = clear). Drive an LED on GPIO22 high when BOTH sensors read 0. Poll the sensors every 100 ms and log each sample to a comma-separated file 'obstacle_log.csv' with columns timestamp,sensor1,sensor2,led_state, flushing after each write. Check every libgpiod call, handle the case where gpiochip0 is unavailable, and verify the log file opens successfully. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown by turning off the LED, releasing all line resources, closing the chip, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to sample a TDK InvenSense ICS-40180 analog MEMS microphone via direct GPIO polling and trigger an LED as a visual alert on sound peaks. The microphone's analog output is fed to GPIO4 (physical pin 7), configured as a digital input, so the program treats the mic line as a binary signal: a HIGH reading constitutes a detected peak. The LED is wired to GPIO17 (physical pin 11) through a current-limiting resistor. Sample the GPIO4 input at approximately 8 kHz (a 125-microsecond period) using pigpio's gpioDelay for timing. On each HIGH reading, print a millisecond-precision timestamp to stdout and turn the LED on GPIO17 ON for 100 ms, then OFF. Check the gpioInitialise() return value, and check every gpioRead/gpioWrite return value, reporting errors to stderr. Use a volatile sig_atomic_t flag for signal handling, without calling pigpio functions from inside the signal handler itself, and implement clean shutdown on SIGINT: stop sampling, ensure the LED is OFF, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library (not wiringPi) to read a SunFounder 3-Way Tracing Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) connected to GPIO17 (left), GPIO27 (center), and GPIO22 (right), configured as active-low inputs with pull-up enabled. Log the left, center, and right sensor states to the console every 100 ms. Implement robust error handling for GPIO initialization failures, line request failures, and read errors, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface to read a Silicon Labs Si1175 optical heart-rate sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x49. Read the ALS visible data registers, LSB at 0x24 and MSB at 0x25, at 100 ms intervals, combine them into a 16-bit value, and log the raw sensor values to the console. Implement robust error handling for I2C initialization and read failures, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod C library (v1.x API, not wiringPi) to read a Keywish 3-Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) connected to Broadcom GPIO pins 2 (left), 3 (middle), and 4 (right). Poll all three lines every 100 ms and log the sensor values to stdout in the format 'L:<0|1> M:<0|1> R:<0|1>'. Use individual gpiod_line_request_input calls (not the bulk API) to maximize portability across libgpiod versions. Check every libgpiod call, including chip open, line get, line request, and line read, and handle the case where the gpiochip device is absent or permission-denied. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, using signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to terminate gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (v1.x API: gpiod_line, gpiod_chip, gpiod_line_get_value; not wiringPi) to read a TTP226 8-channel capacitive touch sensor, whose 8 independent active-high output lines TP1-TP8 connect to BCM GPIO 5, 6, 13, 19, 26, 12, 16, and 20 respectively. Open gpiochip0 and request all 8 lines as inputs. Poll every 200 ms and log each channel's state (0 or 1) to the console in a single timestamped line using a monotonic clock, for example '[12.345s] CH1=0 CH2=1 CH3=0 CH4=0 CH5=0 CH6=0 CH7=0 CH8=0'. Handle errors at every step, including chip-open failure, line-request failure, and individual line-read failure, printing to stderr and exiting with non-zero status. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown that releases all libgpiod resources (lines, chip) cleanly before exiting. Provide compile instructions in a comment.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to create a standalone 'mood lamp' with a common-anode RGB LED connected to GPIO17 (Red), GPIO18 (Green), and GPIO27 (Blue). Smoothly fade between randomly chosen hues every 5 seconds using hardware PWM at 1000 Hz with an 8-bit (0-255) range, applying a 50-step linear interpolation over each 5-second fade. Because the LED is common-anode, invert every PWM duty-cycle value as 255 minus the value, and clamp all color channel values to [0, 255]. Convert each random hue to RGB using the standard HSV-to-RGB algorithm with full saturation and value; select hues internally via rand() seeded from /dev/urandom, with no networking or external message bus required. Check pigpio initialization and every gpioPWM/gpioSetMode return value, logging errors via syslog. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by turning off the LED, releasing pigpio resources, and closing syslog.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library for GPIO control and the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface (not wiringPi) to interface with a TCS34725 color sensor over I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 (BCM pins 2/3) at its fixed address 0x29. Initialize the sensor by powering it on (PON) and enabling RGBC (AEN), set the integration time to approximately 154 ms (ATIME=0x00) and gain to 1x (CONTROL=0x00), and verify the sensor ID register (0x12) returns 0x44 before proceeding. Read all four 16-bit channel registers as little-endian pairs: clear (0x14), red (0x16), green (0x18), and blue (0x1A). Apply per-channel gain and offset calibration and display the calibrated RGB and clear (C) values on the console. Drive an LED on GPIO17 HIGH when the calibrated red value exceeds a threshold of 200, and LOW otherwise. Check every open, ioctl, read, and write return value; attempt sensor re-initialization on a read failure. Ensure clean resource release, closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and powering down the sensor, on all exit paths including SIGINT and SIGTERM. Poll the sensor every 200 ms.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to control the brightness of a 10-LED WS2812B strip connected to GPIO18 (PCM_CLK/GPIO18), generating the precise WS2812B timing waveform via pigpio's hardware PWM/wave functionality. Read ambient light levels from a BH1750 I2C digital light sensor at address 0x23 using continuous high-resolution mode (command 0x10): wait approximately 180 ms after issuing the command, then read 2 bytes and compute lux = (MSB<<8 | LSB) / 1.2. Implement a smooth, non-linear (logarithmic) brightness mapping from the light-sensor readings (0-1000 lux) to LED strip brightness. Gracefully handle I2C errors and sensor-absent conditions with retries, and cleanly release all resources on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 and adjusts the brightness of an APA102 LED strip via SPI proportionally to the measured lux. Use the Linux I2C (/dev/i2c-1) and SPI (/dev/spidev0.0) character devices directly; do not use the deprecated wiringPi library. Initialize the BH1750 in One-Time High-Resolution mode (command 0x20), wait approximately 120 ms for the conversion to complete, then read the 2-byte result and convert to lux using lux = raw / 1.2. Map the lux range [10, 300] to the APA102's 5-bit global brightness [0, 31]. Send an APA102 frame consisting of a 32-bit zero start frame, one 32-bit LED frame per LED (0xE0 | brightness, blue, green, red), and a 32-bit 0xFF end frame, using a 1 MHz SPI clock. Handle SIGINT gracefully by turning off the LEDs and closing all file descriptors. Implement robust error handling for all I/O operations, sensor-absent scenarios, and bus errors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for both I2C communication and SPI output to control an APA102 RGB LED strip's overall brightness based on ambient light from up to three BH1750 I2C light sensors on I2C bus 1, at addresses 0x23 (ADDR low) and 0x5C (ADDR high); attempt to open both addresses and gracefully skip any sensor that is not present. The APA102 strip connects via hardware SPI: MOSI on GPIO10 and SCLK on GPIO11. Average the lux readings across available sensors, ignoring any that report read errors, and map the average lux to a global brightness level (0-31) for the strip, where lower ambient light yields higher brightness. Smoothly fade the strip's global brightness to the new target over 500 ms, looping continuously with a 100 ms delay between cycles. Check all pigpio initialization and I2C/SPI calls for errors, and handle sensor-absent and I2C bus-error paths gracefully. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library for GPIO and the standard Linux i2c-dev interface for I2C (not wiringPi or any deprecated library) to control the brightness of a WS2812B LED strip based on readings from a VEML7700 ambient light sensor at I2C address 0x10. Initialize the VEML7700 with configuration register 0x00 set to 0x0000 (integration time 100 ms, gain 1/8) and read the ALS data from register 0x04 (16-bit). Convert the raw value to lux using lux = raw * 0.0036 * (1/gain) * (100ms/integration_time), which for the default settings reduces to lux = raw * 0.0288. Map the lux value (range 0 to 120000) to LED brightness (0-255) using gamma correction: brightness = 255 * pow(lux / 120000.0, 1.0/2.2). Drive the WS2812B strip via a single GPIO18 pin, bit-banging with libgpiod: toggle the pin at a high frequency such as 800 kHz with duty cycle proportional to brightness, or fall back to threshold-based on/off control if bit-banging is not feasible. Gracefully handle I2C errors, such as sensor absence or bus errors, by retrying up to 3 times with a 100 ms delay between retries, then logging an error and continuing. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly release GPIO lines, close I2C file descriptors, and turn off the LED strip. Run in an infinite loop with a 200 ms delay between iterations, printing the current lux and brightness values to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (gpiod_line_* functions; no sysfs, no wiringPi, no pigpio) to interface with a KY-026 flame sensor (digital output, active-low) on GPIO4. Upon flame detection (sensor output LOW), activate a buzzer on GPIO17 and an LED on GPIO18. On startup, run a self-test: blink the LED twice (500 ms on, 500 ms off) with the buzzer off, then read the flame sensor 5 times at 100 ms intervals; if it consistently reads LOW (flame detected) all 5 times, treat it as a sensor fault. On self-test failure, signal the error with a distinct pattern -- the LED blinking rapidly (100 ms on/off) for 5 cycles, then the buzzer sounding a short-short-long-short pattern (200 ms, 200 ms, 600 ms, 200 ms) repeated 3 times -- then exit with code 1. After self-test passes, poll the flame sensor every 50 ms in the main loop; when flame is detected (LOW), activate the buzzer and LED continuously until the sensor reads HIGH for at least one sample, then deactivate them. Log all events (flame detected, flame gone, errors) with timestamps. Check every gpiod call, including line requests and value reads/writes, and handle failures gracefully with clear error messages. Clean up all GPIO lines on normal exit and on SIGINT (Ctrl+C) using a signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Linux i2c-dev interface (not sysfs) to read ambient light from a BH1750 digital light sensor at I2C address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, initialized in continuous high-resolution mode (command 0x10).
